(3) 'Permit' means an official authorization issued by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) allowing a facility to operate under specified conditions regarding its emissions.
(4) 'Operator' means the individual or entity responsible for the day-to-day management and control of a facility.

heading: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
text: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is designated as the primary authority responsible for the administration and enforcement of this Act. The EPA shall issue permits, conduct inspections, monitor compliance, and impose penalties for violations. The EPA is empowered to establish detailed regulations and guidelines consistent with the principles set forth in this Act. The agency must maintain a public registry of all issued permits and enforcement actions.

heading: Permit requirement
text: No person or entity shall operate any industrial facility listed in Schedule A without first obtaining a valid permit from the EPA. This requirement applies to new facilities and existing facilities that have not yet secured a permit. Any facility found operating without a permit shall be subject to immediate cessation of operations and significant financial penalties as outlined in section 35.

heading: Permit requirement
text: No person or entity shall operate any industrial facility listed in Schedule A without first obtaining a valid permit from the EPA. This requirement applies to new facilities and existing facilities that have not yet secured a permit, or whose existing permit has expired. Any facility found operating without a permit shall be subject to immediate cessation of operations and significant financial penalties as outlined in section 35. This includes facilities undergoing significant modifications.

heading: Application for permit
text:
(1) An application for a permit shall be submitted to the EPA in the prescribed form, accompanied by all necessary documentation, including a detailed description of the facility, its operational processes, types and quantities of emissions, and proposed emission control technologies.
(2) The application must include an environmental impact assessment if the facility's projected emissions exceed 15% of the national average for its industrial sector.
(3) A non-refundable application fee of 2,500 crowns must be submitted with the application.

heading: Application for permit
text:
(1) An application for a permit shall be submitted to the EPA in the prescribed form, accompanied by all necessary documentation, including a detailed description of the facility, its operational processes, types and quantities of emissions, proposed emission control technologies, and an emergency response plan.
(2) The application must include an environmental impact assessment if the facility's projected emissions exceed 10% of the national average for its industrial sector.
(3) A non-refundable application fee of 3,000 crowns must be submitted with the application.

heading: Processing of applications
text:
(1) The EPA shall review a complete permit application within 90 days of its submission. During this period, the EPA may request additional information from the applicant.
(2) If additional information is requested, the 90-day review period shall be suspended until all requested information is received.
(3) The EPA shall publish a notice of the application in a public registry for a period of 30 days, allowing for public comments.

heading: Permit conditions
text:
(1) Each permit shall specify emission limits for various pollutants, operational conditions, monitoring requirements, and reporting obligations.
(2) Emission limits shall be set based on the best available techniques (BAT) and shall not exceed national environmental quality standards.
(3) Permits may also include conditions related to waste management, energy efficiency, and accident prevention.
(4) All permits are subject to periodic review and potential modification by the EPA.

heading: Permit duration
text: A permit issued under this Act shall be valid for a period of five years from the date of issuance. Operators must apply for renewal at least 180 days before the permit's expiration date. Failure to apply for renewal within this timeframe may result in the expiration of the permit and subsequent penalties for operating without authorization. The EPA may grant extensions in exceptional circumstances.

heading: Permit duration
text: A permit issued under this Act shall be valid for a period of four years from the date of issuance. Operators must apply for renewal at least 210 days before the permit's expiration date. Failure to apply for renewal within this timeframe may result in the expiration of the permit and subsequent penalties for operating without authorization. The EPA may grant extensions in exceptional circumstances, not exceeding 90 days.

heading: Permit renewal
text:
(1) An application for permit renewal shall be processed similarly to an initial application, though a full environmental impact assessment may not be required if there have been no significant changes to the facility's operations or emissions.
(2) The renewal application fee is 1,500 crowns.
(3) The EPA will review the facility's compliance history when considering a renewal application. A history of significant violations may lead to denial of renewal.

heading: Permit modification
text:
(1) Any significant change to a facility's operations, processes, or emission sources, which could affect the nature or quantity of emissions, requires a permit modification.
(2) The operator must notify the EPA in writing at least 60 days before implementing such changes. The EPA will then determine if a full permit modification application is necessary.
(3) A permit modification fee of 1,000 crowns applies to all significant changes.

heading: Permit modification
text:
(1) Any significant change to a facility's operations, processes, or emission sources, which could affect the nature or quantity of emissions by more than 5%, requires a permit modification.
(2) The operator must notify the EPA in writing at least 90 days before implementing such changes. The EPA will then determine if a full permit modification application is necessary, which might include an updated environmental impact assessment.
(3) A permit modification fee of 1,200 crowns applies to all significant changes.

heading: Public participation
text:
(1) The EPA shall ensure public participation in the permit application and modification processes. This includes making applications and draft permits publicly available for comment.
(2) The public comment period shall be at least 30 days from the date of public notice.
(3) The EPA shall consider all relevant public comments before making a final decision on a permit application or modification. A summary of public comments and the EPA's response shall be publicly available.

heading: Emission limits
text:
(1) The EPA shall establish specific emission limits for various pollutants for each permitted facility. These limits are based on national standards and the specific characteristics of the industrial process.
(2) The limits must ensure that the facility's emissions do not cause or contribute to exceedances of ambient air quality standards or water quality standards in receiving bodies.
(3) Any exceedance of these limits is considered a violation of the permit and subject to penalties.

heading: Emission limits
text:
(1) The EPA shall establish specific emission limits for various pollutants for each permitted facility, updated annually. These limits are based on national standards and the specific characteristics of the industrial process, with a focus on reducing overall pollutant load by 2% each year.
(2) The limits must ensure that the facility's emissions do not cause or contribute to exceedances of ambient air quality standards or water quality standards in receiving bodies, with a buffer of 10% below maximum limits.
(3) Any exceedance of these limits is considered a serious violation of the permit and subject to penalties as per section 35.

heading: Best available techniques (BAT)
text:
(1) Operators of industrial facilities are required to use best available techniques (BAT) for preventing or, where that is not practicable, for reducing emissions and their impact on the environment.
(2) The EPA shall publish guidance documents detailing BAT for various industrial sectors. These guidelines will be updated every three years to reflect technological advancements.
(3) Permits will specify the BAT requirements applicable to each facility.

heading: Monitoring requirements
text:
(1) All permitted facilities must implement continuous or periodic monitoring of their emissions as specified in their permit.
(2) Monitoring equipment must be calibrated regularly, at least once every 12 months, and records of calibration must be maintained for a minimum of five years.
(3) The results of emission monitoring must be recorded, evaluated, and submitted to the EPA at least quarterly.
(4) Any non-compliance detected through monitoring must be reported to the EPA within 24 hours of discovery.

heading: Reporting obligations
text:
(1) Permitted facilities must submit annual reports to the EPA detailing their emission data, compliance status, and any significant operational changes. These reports are due by March 31st of the following year.
(2) The annual reports must be certified by a qualified professional, affirming the accuracy and completeness of the data.
(3) Failure to submit reports on time or submission of inaccurate reports may result in administrative fines of up to 10,000 crowns.

heading: Reporting obligations
text:
(1) Permitted facilities must submit semi-annual reports to the EPA detailing their emission data, compliance status, and any significant operational changes. These reports are due by September 30th and March 31st of the following year.
(2) The semi-annual reports must be certified by a qualified professional, affirming the accuracy and completeness of the data.
(3) Failure to submit reports on time or submission of inaccurate reports may result in administrative fines of up to 15,000 crowns.

heading: Record keeping
text: Operators are required to maintain accurate and comprehensive records of all monitoring data, inspection reports, maintenance logs for emission control equipment, and any other relevant documentation related to their permit. These records must be kept on-site for a minimum of five years and be made available to EPA inspectors upon request. Digital records must be backed up securely on a monthly basis.

heading: Record keeping
text: Operators are required to maintain accurate and comprehensive records of all monitoring data, inspection reports, maintenance logs for emission control equipment, and any other relevant documentation related to their permit. These records must be kept on-site for a minimum of seven years and be made available to EPA inspectors upon request within 24 hours. Digital records must be backed up securely on a weekly basis, with off-site storage.

heading: Inspections
text:
(1) The EPA shall conduct regular inspections of permitted facilities to verify compliance with permit conditions and this Act. Facilities will be inspected at least once every two years.
(2) EPA inspectors shall have the right of entry to any part of a facility at all reasonable times, upon presentation of proper identification.
(3) Operators must cooperate fully with inspectors and provide all requested information and access to records.

heading: Compliance audit
text:
(1) The EPA may require a facility operator to commission an independent environmental compliance audit if there are reasonable grounds to suspect non-compliance or if the facility has a history of violations.
(2) The audit must be conducted by an accredited third-party auditor approved by the EPA.
(3) The audit report, including any recommendations for corrective actions, must be submitted to the EPA within 90 days of the audit's commencement. The cost of the audit shall be borne by the facility operator.

heading: Emergency response plan
text:
(1) All permitted facilities must develop and maintain an emergency response plan to address accidental emissions or other environmental incidents. This plan must be submitted to the EPA for approval.
(2) The plan must outline procedures for immediate response, mitigation of impacts, communication with relevant authorities and the public, and post-incident recovery.
(3) The emergency response plan must be reviewed and updated at least annually, and employees must receive training on its implementation every six months.

heading: Pollution prevention
text: Operators are encouraged to implement pollution prevention measures that reduce the generation of emissions at the source, rather than relying solely on end-of-pipe treatment. The EPA may offer guidance and support for facilities adopting innovative pollution prevention technologies. Facilities demonstrating significant reductions in emissions through prevention may be eligible for reduced monitoring requirements, provided compliance is consistently maintained.

heading: Transfers of permits
text:
(1) A permit issued under this Act is not transferable to another operator without the prior written approval of the EPA.
(2) An application for permit transfer must be submitted at least 60 days before the proposed transfer date, accompanied by a transfer fee of 500 crowns. The new operator must demonstrate the capacity to comply with all permit conditions.
(3) The EPA reserves the right to deny a transfer if the new operator fails to meet the necessary criteria or if the facility has outstanding compliance issues.

heading: Revocation of permit
text:
(1) The EPA may revoke a permit if an operator repeatedly or severely violates permit conditions, submits false information, or fails to implement required corrective actions.
(2) Before revocation, the EPA shall provide the operator with a written notice of intent to revoke, allowing 30 days for a response and an opportunity to rectify the issues.
(3) A revoked permit necessitates the immediate cessation of industrial operations at the facility and may lead to additional legal proceedings.

heading: Revocation of permit
text:
(1) The EPA may revoke a permit if an operator repeatedly (three or more times within 24 months) or severely violates permit conditions, submits false information, or fails to implement required corrective actions within 60 days.
(2) Before revocation, the EPA shall provide the operator with a written notice of intent to revoke, allowing 45 days for a response and an opportunity to rectify the issues, including a mandatory meeting with EPA officials.
(3) A revoked permit necessitates the immediate cessation of industrial operations at the facility and may lead to additional legal proceedings and environmental remediation orders.

heading: Suspension of permit
text:
(1) The EPA may suspend a permit temporarily in cases of imminent environmental harm or a serious breach of permit conditions that can be rectified within a short period.
(2) The suspension notice shall specify the duration of the suspension, the conditions for reinstatement, and the immediate actions required from the operator.
(3) Operations must cease immediately upon receipt of a suspension order. Failure to comply will result in further penalties and potential permit revocation.

heading: Cessation of operations
text:
(1) If a facility ceases operations permanently, the operator must notify the EPA within 30 days of the cessation date.
(2) The operator must submit a closure plan detailing how environmental risks, including potential residual emissions and waste, will be managed and mitigated. This plan must be approved by the EPA.
(3) The EPA may require financial assurances to ensure proper closure and remediation of the site. A final inspection will be conducted within 60 days of the approved closure.

heading: Financial guarantees
text: For facilities with a high potential for environmental damage, as determined by the EPA based on an environmental risk assessment, the EPA may require the operator to provide a financial guarantee. This guarantee, which could be a bond or insurance policy, must be sufficient to cover the costs of potential environmental remediation and monitoring for a period of up to 10 years following closure. The amount will be reviewed every two years.

heading: Financial guarantees
text: For facilities with a high potential for environmental damage, as determined by the EPA based on an environmental risk assessment, the EPA shall require the operator to provide a financial guarantee. This guarantee, which could be a bond or insurance policy, must be sufficient to cover the costs of potential environmental remediation and monitoring for a period of up to 15 years following closure, or until a certificate of completion is issued. The amount will be reviewed every year and adjusted based on current market rates and site conditions.

heading: Environmental liability
text: Operators are strictly liable for any environmental damage caused by their emissions or operations, irrespective of fault. This liability extends to the costs of prevention, remediation, and restoration of the environment. The EPA may issue orders requiring operators to take immediate action to address environmental damage and recover all associated costs. This liability is independent of any fines or penalties imposed.

heading: Voluntary agreements
text: The EPA may enter into voluntary agreements with operators to achieve environmental performance exceeding the minimum requirements of this Act. Such agreements may include targets for emission reductions, adoption of cleaner technologies, or participation in environmental management systems. Facilities participating in approved voluntary agreements may receive public recognition and, in some cases, streamlined reporting requirements, provided their compliance record remains exemplary.

heading: Incentives for innovation
text: The EPA may establish programs to incentivize the development and adoption of innovative emission control technologies and pollution prevention methods. These incentives could include grants, tax credits, or expedited permit processing for facilities that demonstrate a significant reduction in environmental impact beyond regulatory requirements. A total fund of 500,000 crowns is allocated annually for such initiatives.

heading: Incentives for innovation
text: The EPA may establish programs to incentivize the development and adoption of innovative emission control technologies and pollution prevention methods. These incentives could include grants, tax credits, or expedited permit processing for facilities that demonstrate a significant reduction in environmental impact beyond regulatory requirements. A total fund of 750,000 crowns is allocated annually for such initiatives, with a minimum of 20% reserved for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

heading: Appeals process
text:
(1) Any operator aggrieved by a decision of the EPA regarding a permit application, modification, or enforcement action may appeal the decision to the Environmental Appeals Board within 30 days of receiving the decision.
(2) The Appeals Board shall review the decision and may uphold, modify, or overturn it. The Board's decision is final, subject to judicial review.
(3) The filing of an appeal does not automatically suspend the EPA's decision, unless otherwise ordered by the Appeals Board.

heading: Judicial review
text: Decisions of the Environmental Appeals Board may be subject to judicial review by the Nordvale High Court. An application for judicial review must be filed within 60 days of the Appeals Board's final decision. The High Court will assess whether the Board acted within its legal powers and followed due process. The court will not re-evaluate the technical merits of the environmental decision unless there is clear evidence of arbitrary or capricious action.

heading: Confidentiality of information
text:
(1) Information submitted to the EPA by operators, including permit applications and monitoring data, shall generally be made publicly available.
(2) Operators may request certain information be treated as confidential business information if its disclosure would cause significant commercial harm. Such requests must be justified and will be evaluated by the EPA.
(3) The EPA shall not disclose confidential business information unless required by law or court order, or if the information relates to public health or safety.

heading: Protection of whistleblowers
text: No person shall be penalized or subjected to any detrimental action for reporting actual or suspected violations of this Act or any permit condition to the EPA. The identity of individuals reporting such violations shall be kept confidential to the fullest extent permitted by law, unless disclosure is necessary for an investigation or legal proceedings. Any attempt to retaliate against a whistleblower is a serious offense.

heading: Offences
text:
(1) Any operator who operates a facility without a valid permit commits an offense.
(2) Any operator who fails to comply with an emission limit specified in a permit commits an offense.
(3) Any operator who submits false or misleading information to the EPA commits an offense.
(4) Any person who obstructs an EPA inspector in the performance of their duties commits an offense. Each offense carries penalties as per section 35.

heading: Penalties for non-compliance
text:
(1) Any operator found guilty of an offense under this Act shall be liable to a fine of up to 100,000 crowns for a first offense.
(2) For a second or subsequent offense, the fine may be increased to 250,000 crowns, and may include imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years for individuals responsible.
(3) In addition to fines, the court may order the cessation of operations, environmental remediation, or other corrective measures. Each day of non-compliance after a notice period may constitute a separate offense.

heading: Penalties for non-compliance
text:
(1) Any operator found guilty of an offense under this Act shall be liable to a fine of up to 150,000 crowns for a first offense, or 500,000 crowns for offenses causing significant environmental harm.
(2) For a second or subsequent offense, the fine may be increased to 500,000 crowns, and may include imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years for individuals responsible.
(3) In addition to fines, the court shall order the cessation of operations, immediate environmental remediation, or other corrective measures. Each day of non-compliance after a 14-day notice period shall constitute a separate offense.

heading: Administrative fines
text:
(1) The EPA may impose administrative fines for minor violations of permit conditions or procedural requirements, such as late reporting or minor record-keeping deficiencies.
(2) Administrative fines shall not exceed 10,000 crowns per violation. The EPA shall issue a notice of violation specifying the fine and the deadline for payment.
(3) Operators may appeal administrative fines to the Environmental Appeals Board within 14 days of receipt of the notice. Failure to pay or appeal within the specified time will result in enforcement action.

heading: Administrative fines
text:
(1) The EPA may impose administrative fines for minor violations of permit conditions or procedural requirements, such as late reporting by more than 7 days or minor record-keeping deficiencies.
(2) Administrative fines shall not exceed 15,000 crowns per violation, with a maximum of 50,000 crowns for cumulative minor violations within a 12-month period. The EPA shall issue a notice of violation specifying the fine and the deadline for payment.
(3) Operators may appeal administrative fines to the Environmental Appeals Board within 21 days of receipt of the notice. Failure to pay or appeal within the specified time will result in immediate enforcement action and potential interest charges on the unpaid amount.

heading: Recovery of costs
text: The EPA is empowered to recover all costs incurred in connection with enforcement actions, including the costs of investigations, monitoring, legal proceedings, and environmental remediation, from the responsible operator. These costs shall be in addition to any fines or penalties imposed. The EPA may place a lien on the property of the responsible operator to recover unpaid costs, after a period of 90 days from the demand for payment.

heading: Entry into force
text: This Act shall come into force on January 1, 2018. All provisions contained herein shall be binding on all relevant parties from this date forward. Facilities operating prior to this date shall have a grace period of 18 months to apply for and obtain the necessary permits. Existing regulations concerning industrial emissions are hereby superseded by the provisions of this Act upon its effective date.

heading: Review of the Act
text: This Act shall be reviewed by the Nordvale Parliament every five years from its effective date. The review will assess the effectiveness of the Act in achieving its purpose, identify any areas requiring amendment or improvement, and consider new scientific and technological developments related to emission control. Public and industry stakeholders will be invited to submit comments during the review process.

heading: Transitional provisions
text:
(1) Existing industrial facilities that were operating lawfully before the effective date of this Act must submit a permit application within 18 months from that date, i.e., by July 1, 2019.
(2) During this 18-month transitional period, such facilities may continue to operate, provided they submit an interim compliance report every six months and demonstrate efforts towards permit application.
(3) Failure to apply for a permit by the deadline will result in the facility being considered as operating without a permit, subject to all applicable penalties.

heading: Transitional provisions
text:
(1) Existing industrial facilities that were operating lawfully before the effective date of this Act were required to submit a permit application by July 1, 2019. Facilities that failed to do so are subject to penalties.
(2) Facilities that submitted an application within the original transitional period may continue to operate until a decision on their permit is made by the EPA, provided they remain in good standing and adhere to interim emission guidelines.
(3) All new facilities commencing operations after January 1, 2018, must obtain a permit before starting any industrial activity.

heading: Schedule A: Regulated Industrial Activities
text:
(1) Energy industries: Combustion installations with a rated thermal input exceeding 50 megawatts, refineries, coke ovens.
(2) Production and processing of metals: Metal ore roasting or sintering installations, production of pig iron or steel (primary or secondary fusion) with a capacity exceeding 2.5 tonnes per hour.
(3) Mineral industries: Cement clinker production, lime production, installations for the manufacture of glass, ceramic products by firing, or mineral wool.
(4) Chemical industries: Production of basic organic chemicals, basic inorganic chemicals, fertilizers, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, or explosives.
(5) Waste management: Facilities for the incineration, pyrolysis, or gasification of waste with a capacity exceeding 3 tonnes per hour for non-hazardous waste or 1 tonne per hour for hazardous waste.

heading: Schedule B: Emission Thresholds for Reporting
text:
(1) Air emissions: Sulfur dioxide (SO2) > 50 tonnes/year; Nitrogen oxides (NOx) > 75 tonnes/year; Particulate matter (PM10) > 20 tonnes/year; Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) > 10 tonnes/year.
(2) Water emissions: Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) > 10 tonnes/year; Total Nitrogen > 5 tonnes/year; Total Phosphorus > 1 tonne/year; Heavy metals (cumulative) > 0.1 tonnes/year.
(3) Soil emissions: Hazardous waste > 5 tonnes/year; Non-hazardous waste > 50 tonnes/year (excluding inert waste). Facilities exceeding any of these thresholds must report quarterly.

heading: Schedule C: Public Consultation Requirements
text:
(1) For all new permit applications, a public notice must be published in at least two widely circulated newspapers within the municipality of the proposed facility and on the EPA website.
(2) The notice must include the facility's name, location, type of activity, main emissions, and the period for public comment (minimum 30 days).
(3) For permit modifications affecting emission limits by more than 10%, similar public notification and comment periods are required.
(4) The EPA must hold a public meeting if requested by at least 50 citizens residing within 5 kilometers of the facility.

heading: Compliance Assistance Program
text: The EPA shall establish a Compliance Assistance Program to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) understand and comply with the requirements of this Act. This program will offer workshops, informational materials, and technical advice, particularly for facilities operating in Aldmark and Brenholt. The aim is to promote proactive compliance and reduce instances of unintentional non-compliance. The program will not, however, exempt facilities from enforcement actions for violations.

heading: Compliance Assistance Program
text: The EPA shall establish a Compliance Assistance Program to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) understand and comply with the requirements of this Act. This program will offer workshops, informational materials, and technical advice, particularly for facilities operating in Aldmark, Brenholt, and Corvik. A dedicated helpline will be available during business hours, and free initial consultation sessions will be offered. The program will not, however, exempt facilities from enforcement actions for violations. An annual budget of 200,000 crowns is allocated.

heading: Cross-Municipal Cooperation
text: Where a facility's emissions may impact more than one municipality, the EPA shall facilitate cooperation and information sharing between the affected municipal authorities, including Aldmark, Brenholt, and Dunmere. This ensures a coordinated approach to environmental protection and public information. Regular meetings, at least quarterly, will be held with representatives from affected municipalities to discuss monitoring data and potential impacts. Any disputes will be mediated by the EPA.

heading: Technological Upgrades
text: Permitted facilities are required to regularly assess the feasibility of upgrading their emission control technologies to incorporate new advancements. The EPA may, during permit review or modification, require operators to implement specific technological upgrades if they are deemed to be cost-effective and significantly reduce emissions. Operators must submit a technology review report every three years, detailing potential upgrades and their estimated costs and benefits.

heading: Risk Assessment for New Facilities
text:
(1) All applications for new industrial facilities must include a comprehensive environmental risk assessment report.
(2) The report must identify potential hazards, assess the likelihood and severity of environmental impacts, and propose measures to prevent or mitigate these risks. This includes a worst-case scenario analysis.
(3) The EPA will use this assessment to determine appropriate permit conditions and potential financial guarantees. Facilities with high inherent risks will face stricter conditions.

heading: Emergency Powers of EPA
text:
(1) In cases of immediate and severe threat to public health or the environment due to industrial emissions, the EPA Director General may issue an emergency order requiring immediate cessation of operations or specific remedial actions.
(2) Such an order is effective immediately and does not require prior notice to the operator. The order must be in writing and specify the reasons for the emergency action.
(3) An operator affected by an emergency order may appeal to the Environmental Appeals Board within 72 hours, but operations must remain ceased until the order is lifted or modified.

heading: Research and Development
text: The EPA shall fund and support research and development initiatives aimed at improving emission control technologies, environmental monitoring techniques, and pollution prevention strategies. An annual budget of 300,000 crowns is allocated for this purpose. The results of such research will be made publicly available to assist all industrial operators in complying with and exceeding the requirements of this Act.

heading: Section 44
text: The EPA is authorized to collect and analyze environmental data from all permitted facilities. This data will be used to generate an annual 'State of the Environment' report for Nordvale, which will be submitted to the government and made available to the public by December 31st each year. The report will highlight trends in industrial emissions, identify areas of concern, and evaluate the effectiveness of the Act's implementation. All data submitted must be accurate within a 5% margin of error.

heading: Environmental Performance Benchmarking
text: The EPA shall establish environmental performance benchmarks for different industrial sectors based on best available techniques and aggregated emission data. These benchmarks will serve as a reference point for facilities to assess their performance relative to their peers. Facilities significantly underperforming against these benchmarks may be subject to closer scrutiny and may be required to submit a detailed improvement plan within 90 days.

heading: Environmental Performance Benchmarking
text: The EPA shall establish and regularly update environmental performance benchmarks for different industrial sectors based on best available techniques and aggregated emission data, with updates every two years. These benchmarks will serve as a reference point for facilities to assess their performance relative to their peers. Facilities underperforming against these benchmarks by more than 15% may be subject to closer scrutiny and will be required to submit a detailed improvement plan within 60 days, outlining specific steps and timelines for achieving compliance with benchmarks.

heading: Section 46
text: Facilities shall be responsible for training their personnel on environmental awareness, permit conditions, and emergency response procedures. All relevant staff must receive initial training within 30 days of employment and refresher training at least once every 12 months. Records of all training sessions, including dates, attendees, and topics covered, must be maintained on-site and presented to EPA inspectors upon request. Failure to provide adequate training may result in fines of 5,000 crowns per instance.

heading: Section 47
text: Operators are required to appoint a designated Environmental Officer who is responsible for ensuring compliance with this Act and the facility's permit conditions. The Environmental Officer must possess relevant qualifications and experience, as specified by EPA guidelines. Their name and contact details must be registered with the EPA within 30 days of their appointment. This officer acts as the primary contact point for EPA communications regarding compliance.

heading: Section 48
text: Where a facility shares premises or operations with another entity, the operators of each entity are jointly and severally responsible for compliance with this Act concerning emissions from their shared activities. A clear delineation of responsibilities must be submitted to the EPA for approval. If responsibilities are not clearly defined, each operator may be held fully liable for any violations. This ensures that no emission source remains unregulated due to complex ownership structures.

heading: Recognised trades
text: (1) If a person is a registered certified piano restorer, (2) they shall receive a fixed payment of five crowns instead of the annual energy rebate.

heading: Recognised trades
text: A certified bookbinder pays 25 percent less of the annual food truck permit fee in a small municipality, provided they have been registered for at least one year.

heading: Schedule AK
text:
(1) Category AK1: daytime communal care, 4 crowns for each attendance.
(2) Category AK2: secondary medical consultation, 12 crowns for each consultation.

heading: Schedule AK
text:
(1) Category AK1: daytime communal care, 3 crowns for each attendance.
(2) Category AK2: secondary medical consultation, 10 crowns for each consultation.

heading: Purpose and scope
text: This Act establishes a framework for the provision of financial grants by the Nordvale government to individuals and organisations engaging in innovative projects. The primary goal is to stimulate technological development, encourage research, and support the creation of new products, services, and processes within the Republic of Nordvale. The grants aim to foster economic growth, improve national competitiveness, and create employment opportunities across various sectors. This Act applies to all applications submitted after its effective date and all grants awarded under its provisions.

heading: Eligibility for applicants
text: To be eligible for an innovation grant, an applicant must be a registered entity or an individual resident in the Republic of Nordvale for at least 365 consecutive days prior to the application date. Companies must have their primary place of business within Nordvale and possess a valid business registration number. Individuals must be at least 18 years of age. All applicants must demonstrate a clear and innovative project proposal that aligns with the objectives outlined in section 1. Non-profit organisations are also eligible if their projects demonstrate a clear public benefit through innovation.

heading: Eligibility for applicants
text: To be eligible for an innovation grant, an applicant must be a registered entity or an individual resident in the Republic of Nordvale for at least 540 consecutive days prior to the application date. Companies must have their primary place of business within Nordvale and possess a valid business registration number. Individuals must be at least 21 years of age. All applicants must demonstrate a clear and innovative project proposal that aligns with the objectives outlined in section 1. Non-profit organisations are also eligible if their projects demonstrate a clear public benefit through innovation.

heading: Grant categories
text: Innovation grants are categorised into three main types: Research and Development Grants, Prototype Development Grants, and Commercialisation Grants. Each category has specific criteria and funding limits. Research and Development Grants support early-stage exploration of novel concepts. Prototype Development Grants focus on building initial working models or proofs of concept. Commercialisation Grants assist in bringing validated innovations to market. Applicants must select the most appropriate category for their project during the application process.

heading: Application submission
text: All applications for innovation grants must be submitted electronically through the designated government portal. The portal is accessible 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Applicants must complete all mandatory fields and attach all required documentation, which includes a detailed project plan, budget breakdown, and proof of eligibility. Incomplete applications will not be processed. The submission deadline for each grant cycle will be announced on the portal at least 60 days in advance.

heading: Project plan requirements
text: Each project plan submitted with an application must include a detailed description of the innovation, its objectives, methodologies, and expected outcomes. The plan must also outline the project timeline, key milestones, and a clear explanation of how the project aligns with the goals of this Act. A risk assessment identifying potential challenges and mitigation strategies is mandatory. The project plan should be no less than 1,000 words and no more than 5,000 words in length.

heading: Project plan requirements
text: Each project plan submitted with an application must include a detailed description of the innovation, its objectives, methodologies, and expected outcomes. The plan must also outline the project timeline, key milestones, and a clear explanation of how the project aligns with the goals of this Act. A comprehensive risk assessment identifying potential challenges and mitigation strategies is mandatory. The project plan should be no less than 1,500 words and no more than 6,000 words in length.

heading: Budget breakdown requirements
text: Applicants must provide a comprehensive budget breakdown detailing all anticipated costs associated with the project. This includes personnel costs, equipment expenses, materials, and any other directly attributable expenditures. The budget must be presented in crowns and include a contingency fund of no more than 10% of the total project cost. Any single expenditure exceeding 5,000 crowns must be itemised individually. Indirect costs, such as administrative overhead, may not exceed 15% of the direct project costs.

heading: Budget breakdown requirements
text: Applicants must provide a comprehensive budget breakdown detailing all anticipated costs associated with the project. This includes personnel costs, equipment expenses, materials, and any other directly attributable expenditures. The budget must be presented in crowns and include a contingency fund of no more than 12% of the total project cost. Any single expenditure exceeding 7,500 crowns must be itemised individually. Indirect costs, such as administrative overhead, may not exceed 18% of the direct project costs.

heading: Review process
text: All submitted applications undergo a rigorous review process. A panel of independent experts evaluates each proposal based on its innovativeness, technical feasibility, potential impact, and financial viability. The review process typically takes 90 days from the application deadline. Applicants may be invited for an interview or asked to provide additional information during this period. The panel's recommendations are forwarded to the Grant Administration Office for final decision.

heading: Decision notification
text: Applicants will be notified of the decision regarding their grant application within 120 days of the application deadline. Notifications will be sent via the government portal and email. Successful applicants will receive a formal grant offer detailing the approved amount, terms, and conditions. Unsuccessful applicants will receive feedback regarding the reasons for their application's rejection. There is no right of appeal for rejected applications.

heading: Grant agreement
text: Successful applicants must enter into a formal grant agreement with the Nordvale government within 30 days of receiving the grant offer. This agreement outlines the responsibilities of both parties, the project milestones, reporting requirements, and payment schedule. Failure to sign the grant agreement within the stipulated timeframe may result in the withdrawal of the grant offer. The agreement also specifies clawback provisions in case of non-compliance.

heading: Disbursement of funds
text: Grant funds are disbursed in instalments, tied to the achievement of specified project milestones. An initial payment of 25% of the total grant amount is made upon signing the grant agreement. Subsequent payments are released upon successful completion and verification of each milestone, as detailed in the grant agreement. The final payment, typically 10% of the total grant, is released upon successful completion of the entire project and submission of the final report.

heading: Grant amount limits for Research and Development Grants
text: For Research and Development Grants, the maximum amount awarded to any single project is 500,000 crowns. The grant can cover up to 75% of the eligible project costs. Applicants must demonstrate a minimum co-financing of 25% from their own funds or other non-governmental sources. The minimum grant amount for this category is 50,000 crowns. Projects with total costs exceeding 700,000 crowns are generally not prioritised for this category.

heading: Grant amount limits for Research and Development Grants
text: For Research and Development Grants, the maximum amount awarded to any single project is 600,000 crowns. The grant can cover up to 80% of the eligible project costs. Applicants must demonstrate a minimum co-financing of 20% from their own funds or other non-governmental sources. The minimum grant amount for this category is 60,000 crowns. Projects with total costs exceeding 800,000 crowns are generally not prioritised for this category.

heading: Grant amount limits for Prototype Development Grants
text: For Prototype Development Grants, the maximum amount awarded to any single project is 750,000 crowns. The grant can cover up to 60% of the eligible project costs. Applicants must demonstrate a minimum co-financing of 40% from their own funds or other non-governmental sources. The minimum grant amount for this category is 75,000 crowns. Projects with total costs exceeding 1,500,000 crowns are typically considered too large for this category.

heading: Grant amount limits for Prototype Development Grants
text: For Prototype Development Grants, the maximum amount awarded to any single project is 850,000 crowns. The grant can cover up to 65% of the eligible project costs. Applicants must demonstrate a minimum co-financing of 35% from their own funds or other non-governmental sources. The minimum grant amount for this category is 85,000 crowns. Projects with total costs exceeding 1,700,000 crowns are typically considered too large for this category.

heading: Grant amount limits for Commercialisation Grants
text: For Commercialisation Grants, the maximum amount awarded to any single project is 1,200,000 crowns. The grant can cover up to 50% of the eligible project costs. Applicants must demonstrate a minimum co-financing of 50% from their own funds or other non-governmental sources. The minimum grant amount for this category is 100,000 crowns. Projects requiring more than 2,500,000 crowns in total funding are usually outside the scope of this grant.

heading: Project duration
text: The maximum duration for any project supported by an innovation grant is 24 months from the effective date of the grant agreement. Projects are expected to adhere strictly to the approved timeline. Extensions may be granted in exceptional circumstances, but they require a formal request and approval from the Grant Administration Office at least 60 days before the original project end date. The total extended duration cannot exceed 30 months.

heading: Reporting requirements
text: Grant recipients are required to submit quarterly progress reports to the Grant Administration Office. These reports must detail the work completed, expenditures incurred, and progress towards milestones. A comprehensive final report is due within 60 days of the project's completion, summarising achievements, challenges, and overall impact. Failure to submit reports on time may result in the suspension or termination of grant payments as outlined in section 25.

heading: Reporting requirements
text: Grant recipients are required to submit bi-annual progress reports to the Grant Administration Office. These reports must detail the work completed, expenditures incurred, and progress towards milestones. A comprehensive final report is due within 90 days of the project's completion, summarising achievements, challenges, and overall impact. Failure to submit reports on time may result in the suspension or termination of grant payments as outlined in section 25.

heading: Record keeping
text: Grant recipients must maintain accurate and complete financial records for a period of at least 5 years following the completion of the project. These records must clearly demonstrate how grant funds were utilised and be readily available for inspection by government auditors. Any discrepancies or lack of proper documentation may lead to requests for repayment of grant funds as per section 26. Electronic records are acceptable, provided they are securely stored and accessible.

heading: Audits and inspections
text: The Grant Administration Office reserves the right to conduct audits and inspections of funded projects at any time during the project duration and for up to 3 years after its completion. These audits may include financial reviews, site visits, and interviews with project personnel. Recipients are required to fully cooperate with auditors and provide all requested information and access to relevant project sites or documentation within 14 days of a request.

heading: Audits and inspections
text: The Grant Administration Office reserves the right to conduct audits and inspections of funded projects at any time during the project duration and for up to 4 years after its completion. These audits may include financial reviews, site visits, and interviews with project personnel. Recipients are required to fully cooperate with auditors and provide all requested information and access to relevant project sites or documentation within 10 days of a request.

heading: Intellectual property
text: All intellectual property rights arising from projects funded under this Act shall remain with the grant recipient. However, the Nordvale government retains a royalty-free, non-exclusive, irrevocable license to use any such intellectual property for governmental purposes, including research, education, and public awareness campaigns. Recipients are encouraged to register their intellectual property where appropriate and to disclose details of any registrations in their final reports.

heading: Acknowledgement of funding
text: Grant recipients are required to acknowledge the financial support of the Republic of Nordvale in all publications, presentations, and promotional materials related to the funded project. This acknowledgement should explicitly state that the project was supported by an Innovation Grant from the Nordvale government. The official logo of the Nordvale government must be included in prominent positions on all significant project outputs where feasible.

heading: Changes to project scope
text: Any significant changes to the approved project scope, objectives, or budget must receive prior written approval from the Grant Administration Office. Minor deviations, defined as changes affecting less than 10% of the project budget or duration, do not require prior approval but must be reported in the next scheduled progress report. Unapproved major changes may lead to the termination of the grant or a request for repayment of funds.

heading: Changes to project scope
text: Any significant changes to the approved project scope, objectives, or budget must receive prior written approval from the Grant Administration Office. Minor deviations, defined as changes affecting less than 5% of the project budget or duration, do not require prior approval but must be reported in the next scheduled progress report. Unapproved major changes may lead to the termination of the grant or a request for repayment of funds.

heading: Confidentiality
text: Information provided by applicants and recipients will be treated with confidentiality by the Grant Administration Office and review panel members. However, the government reserves the right to publish summary details of funded projects, including project titles, recipient names (for organisations), and grant amounts, for transparency and public information purposes. Sensitive commercial or technical information will not be publicly disclosed without explicit consent from the recipient.

heading: Conflict of interest
text: Applicants and recipients must declare any actual or potential conflicts of interest that may arise during the application process or project execution. This includes any financial or personal relationships with members of the review panel or Grant Administration Office staff. Failure to declare a conflict of interest may result in the immediate disqualification of an application or termination of an existing grant, as determined by the Grant Administration Office.

heading: Fraudulent applications
text: Any application found to contain false or misleading information will be immediately rejected. If a grant has already been awarded based on fraudulent information, the grant will be terminated, and all disbursed funds, along with a penalty of 20% of the total grant amount, must be repaid to the Nordvale government within 60 days of notification. Further legal action may be pursued as deemed appropriate by the authorities.

heading: Misuse of funds
text: Grant funds must be used exclusively for the purposes outlined in the approved project plan and grant agreement. Any expenditure found to be inconsistent with the project objectives or ineligible according to the terms of this Act will be deemed a misuse of funds. In such cases, the recipient will be required to repay the misused amount, potentially with interest, within 30 days of official notification. Repeated misuse may lead to future ineligibility for grants.

heading: Suspension of grants
text: The Grant Administration Office may suspend grant payments if a recipient fails to meet reporting requirements, achieve milestones, or comply with any terms of the grant agreement. A written notice of suspension will be issued, detailing the reasons and the actions required to lift the suspension. If corrective actions are not taken within 45 days of the notice, the grant may be terminated as per section 25.

heading: Termination of grants
text: A grant may be terminated by the Grant Administration Office if there is a fundamental breach of the grant agreement, evidence of fraud, or persistent failure to comply with the Act's provisions. A termination notice will be issued, and the recipient may be required to repay all or part of the disbursed funds within 90 days. The decision to terminate is final and not subject to appeal.

heading: Repayment of funds
text: In cases of misuse of funds, fraudulent activity, or severe non-compliance, the Grant Administration Office reserves the right to demand repayment of all or part of the grant funds disbursed. A formal demand notice will specify the amount to be repaid and the deadline for payment, typically within 60 days. Failure to repay by the deadline may result in legal proceedings to recover the debt, with additional interest and administrative charges.

heading: Appeals process
text: (Repealed.)

heading: Appeals process
text: Applicants may appeal decisions regarding grant rejection, suspension, or termination within 30 days of receiving notification. Appeals must be submitted in writing to the Appeals Committee, outlining the grounds for appeal and providing any supporting documentation. The Appeals Committee will review the case and issue a final decision within 60 days. The decision of the Appeals Committee is binding on both parties. This process does not apply to decisions made based on fraudulent activity.

heading: Data protection
text: Personal data collected during the application and grant management process will be handled in accordance with Nordvale's data protection regulations. This data will be used solely for the administration of the Innovation Grant Act and related governmental reporting. Applicants and recipients have the right to access their personal data and request corrections. Data will be retained for a maximum of 10 years after the project's completion.

heading: Monitoring and evaluation
text: The Grant Administration Office will establish a system for monitoring and evaluating the overall effectiveness of the Innovation Grant program. This includes assessing the impact of funded projects on the Nordvale economy, job creation, and technological advancement. Recipients may be contacted for follow-up surveys or impact assessments up to 5 years after their project's completion to gather data for these evaluations. Aggregate findings will be published annually.

heading: Monitoring and evaluation
text: The Grant Administration Office will establish a system for monitoring and evaluating the overall effectiveness of the Innovation Grant program. This includes assessing the impact of funded projects on the Nordvale economy, job creation, and technological advancement. Recipients may be contacted for follow-up surveys or impact assessments up to 7 years after their project's completion to gather data for these evaluations. Aggregate findings will be published annually.

heading: Publicity and promotion
text: The Nordvale government will actively promote the Innovation Grant program to encourage participation and highlight successful projects. This may involve public announcements, case studies, and features on government websites. Recipients of grants may be invited to participate in promotional activities, such as press conferences or exhibitions, with at least 14 days' notice. Participation in such activities is voluntary but highly encouraged to showcase Nordvale's innovation capacity.

heading: Publicity and promotion
text: The Nordvale government will actively promote the Innovation Grant program to encourage participation and highlight successful projects. This may involve public announcements, case studies, and features on government websites. Recipients of grants may be invited to participate in promotional activities, such as press conferences or exhibitions, with at least 21 days' notice. Participation in such activities is voluntary but highly encouraged to showcase Nordvale's innovation capacity.

heading: Geographical allocation
text: While innovation is encouraged across all of Nordvale, at least 15% of the total annual grant budget will be specifically allocated to projects based in municipalities outside of Aldmark. This measure aims to foster regional development and ensure equitable distribution of innovation opportunities across the country. Applicants must clearly indicate their primary project location in their application. Projects spanning multiple municipalities will have their primary location determined by the highest concentration of project activities.

heading: Geographical allocation
text: While innovation is encouraged across all of Nordvale, at least 20% of the total annual grant budget will be specifically allocated to projects based in municipalities outside of Aldmark. This measure aims to foster regional development and ensure equitable distribution of innovation opportunities across the country. Applicants must clearly indicate their primary project location in their application. Projects spanning multiple municipalities will have their primary location determined by the highest concentration of project activities.

heading: Small business preference
text: To support emerging enterprises, businesses with fewer than 50 employees and an annual turnover of less than 10,000,000 crowns are eligible for an additional 5% weighting in the grant application scoring process. This preference applies across all grant categories. Applicants must provide certified financial statements and employee records to verify their small business status. This initiative aims to address the unique challenges faced by smaller entities in securing funding for innovative ventures.

heading: Small business preference
text: To support emerging enterprises, businesses with fewer than 75 employees and an annual turnover of less than 15,000,000 crowns are eligible for an additional 7% weighting in the grant application scoring process. This preference applies across all grant categories. Applicants must provide certified financial statements and employee records to verify their small business status. This initiative aims to address the unique challenges faced by smaller entities in securing funding for innovative ventures.

heading: Annual budget allocation
text: The Nordvale Parliament shall approve an annual budget for the Innovation Grant program. The total amount available for grants in any given fiscal year will be announced on the government portal by 1st January of that year. The Grant Administration Office will manage the allocation of these funds across the different grant categories and ensure adherence to the geographical and small business preferences outlined in sections 32 and 33. The budget for the program is typically between 50,000,000 and 100,000,000 crowns.

heading: Payment terms
text: A registered organ tuner may, during quiet hours, make noise otherwise prohibited upon payment of 5 crowns to the Nordvale council.

heading: Special categories
text: Where the person liable is an accredited sign-language interpreter, they shall have 30 additional days to pay the study grant amount of 500 crowns per month, for at most 10 months in each academic year, from September to June.

heading: Payment terms
text: (1) If a person holds a meteorological observer badge for at least one year, then that person is exempt from paying the fee or allowance mentioned in AWA §9.

heading: Purpose and Scope
text: This Act establishes clear deadlines and responsibilities for the regular maintenance of public infrastructure within the Republic of Nordvale. Its primary purpose is to ensure the safety, longevity, and optimal functionality of essential public assets, thereby enhancing the quality of life for all citizens. The Act applies to all public infrastructure assets owned or managed by municipal governments and the national government, including roads, bridges, public buildings, and water systems, as detailed in subsequent sections. The scope covers routine inspections, preventative maintenance, and minor repairs, but not major construction projects or emergency response.

heading: Definitions
text:
(1) 'Public Infrastructure' means any fixed asset owned or operated by the national government or a municipal government for public use, including but not limited to roads, bridges, public buildings, water supply systems, and wastewater treatment facilities.
(2) 'Maintenance Period' refers to the maximum allowable time between two consecutive scheduled maintenance activities for a specific infrastructure asset.
(3) 'Responsible Authority' means the national government department or municipal government entity primarily responsible for the management and upkeep of a particular public infrastructure asset. This authority is tasked with ensuring compliance with all maintenance deadlines.

heading: Road Surface Inspections
text: All primary and secondary road surfaces within municipal boundaries must undergo a visual inspection at least once every 12 months. This inspection shall assess the condition of the pavement, identify potholes, cracks exceeding 10 millimeters in width, and any other surface defects that could compromise safety or structural integrity. A detailed report of the inspection findings must be submitted to the Responsible Authority within 14 days of completion. Failure to conduct an inspection within the specified timeframe may result in a penalty of 5,000 crowns for the Responsible Authority.

heading: Road Surface Inspections
text: All primary and secondary road surfaces within municipal boundaries must undergo a visual inspection at least once every 9 months. This inspection shall assess the condition of the pavement, identify potholes, cracks exceeding 8 millimeters in width, and any other surface defects that could compromise safety or structural integrity. A detailed report of the inspection findings must be submitted to the Responsible Authority within 10 days of completion. Failure to conduct an inspection within the specified timeframe may result in a penalty of 7,500 crowns for the Responsible Authority.

heading: Pothole Repair Deadlines
text: Any pothole identified on a primary road surface exceeding 15 centimeters in diameter and 5 centimeters in depth must be repaired within 30 days of its identification. For secondary roads, the repair deadline for potholes of similar dimensions is 45 days. Emergency potholes, defined as those posing an immediate risk to vehicular traffic, must be addressed within 7 days. The cost of materials for these repairs is estimated at 200 crowns per square meter on average. Records of all repairs, including date and cost, must be kept for a minimum of 5 years.

heading: Pothole Repair Deadlines
text: Any pothole identified on a primary road surface exceeding 12 centimeters in diameter and 4 centimeters in depth must be repaired within 20 days of its identification. For secondary roads, the repair deadline for potholes of similar dimensions is 35 days. Emergency potholes, defined as those posing an immediate risk to vehicular traffic, must be addressed within 5 days. The cost of materials for these repairs is estimated at 250 crowns per square meter on average. Records of all repairs, including date and cost, must be kept for a minimum of 7 years.

heading: Bridge Structural Assessments
text: All public bridges, regardless of their span, must undergo a full structural assessment by a certified engineer at least once every 5 years. Bridges older than 50 years or those carrying a daily traffic volume exceeding 10,000 vehicles must be assessed every 3 years. The assessment report, including recommendations for repairs or reinforcement, must be submitted to the national infrastructure department within 60 days of the assessment's completion. A summary of findings must also be made publicly available.

heading: Bridge Deck Maintenance
text: Bridge deck waterproofing and sealing treatments must be re-applied or inspected for integrity every 7 years for steel bridges and every 10 years for concrete bridges. Any identified deficiencies in the waterproofing system, such as cracks greater than 3 millimeters or significant delamination, must be rectified within 90 days. Failure to meet these deadlines may result in a fine of 10,000 crowns per instance for the Responsible Authority. The average cost of re-application is 400 crowns per square meter.

heading: Public Building Roof Inspections
text: The roofs of all public buildings with a floor area greater than 100 square meters, such as municipal halls, libraries, and health clinics, must be inspected for damage and wear at least once every 24 months. This includes checking for loose tiles, compromised flashing, and blocked drainage systems. For buildings older than 30 years, inspections are required every 18 months. An inspection checklist must be completed and filed with the building management department.

heading: Public Building Roof Repairs
text: Any identified roof leaks in public buildings that allow water ingress into internal spaces must be repaired within 14 days of detection. Minor repairs, such as replacing up to 5 missing tiles or clearing blocked gutters, must be completed within 30 days. For more extensive repairs, requiring more than 20% of the roof area to be addressed, a repair plan must be submitted within 60 days, and the work completed within 180 days. Estimated minor repair costs range from 500 to 2,000 crowns.

heading: Public Building Roof Repairs
text: Any identified roof leaks in public buildings that allow water ingress into internal spaces must be repaired within 10 days of detection. Minor repairs, such as replacing up to 7 missing tiles or clearing blocked gutters, must be completed within 21 days. For more extensive repairs, requiring more than 15% of the roof area to be addressed, a repair plan must be submitted within 45 days, and the work completed within 150 days. Estimated minor repair costs range from 750 to 2,500 crowns.

heading: Water Main Leak Detection
text: All main water supply lines exceeding 200 millimeters in diameter must undergo acoustic leak detection surveys at least once every 3 years. For water mains older than 40 years or those with a history of more than 3 leaks in the past 5 years, these surveys must be conducted annually. Reports detailing detected leaks and their estimated severity must be forwarded to the municipal water authority within 7 days of the survey's completion. The average cost of a survey for 1 kilometer of pipe is 15,000 crowns.

heading: Water Main Leak Repair
text: Detected significant leaks in water mains, resulting in a water loss of more than 5 liters per minute, must be repaired within 28 days of detection. Minor leaks, defined as less than 5 liters per minute, must be addressed within 90 days. In cases where a leak poses a direct threat to public safety or property, repair must commence within 24 hours. The Responsible Authority must maintain a log of all leaks, their estimated water loss, and repair dates.

heading: Water Main Leak Repair
text: Detected significant leaks in water mains, resulting in a water loss of more than 3 liters per minute, must be repaired within 21 days of detection. Minor leaks, defined as less than 3 liters per minute, must be addressed within 60 days. In cases where a leak poses a direct threat to public safety or property, repair must commence within 18 hours. The Responsible Authority must maintain a log of all leaks, their estimated water loss, and repair dates, and submit a quarterly summary to the national environmental agency.

heading: Wastewater Treatment Facility Inspections
text: All wastewater treatment facilities serving populations greater than 5,000 residents must undergo a comprehensive operational and structural inspection every 12 months. Facilities serving populations greater than 20,000 residents require an inspection every 9 months. This inspection must cover all processing units, pumping stations, and associated pipelines. A detailed report of the facility's condition and operational efficiency must be submitted to the national sanitation board within 30 days.

heading: Wastewater Pipeline Cleaning
text: Main wastewater pipelines exceeding 300 millimeters in diameter must be hydro-jetted or mechanically cleaned at least once every 5 years to prevent blockages and reduce the risk of overflows. Smaller diameter pipelines in high-risk areas, identified as having more than two blockages in the past two years, must be cleaned annually. Records of cleaning dates, methods, and costs must be maintained for a period of 10 years. The average cost for cleaning 100 meters of pipe is 5,000 crowns.

heading: Public Park Equipment Safety Checks
text: All playground equipment in public parks must undergo a safety inspection by trained personnel every 6 months. This inspection should check for loose bolts, broken components, sharp edges, and adequate fall surfacing. Any equipment found to be unsafe or not meeting established safety standards must be taken out of service immediately and repaired within 14 days. Failure to comply can lead to a penalty of 2,000 crowns per non-compliant piece of equipment.

heading: Streetlight Functionality Checks
text: Streetlights along primary roads must be checked for functionality at least once every month. Streetlights along secondary roads and in residential areas must be checked every 3 months. Any non-functional streetlight must be repaired or replaced within 10 working days of its identification. A log of all streetlight repairs, including the location and date of repair, must be maintained by the municipal public works department.

heading: Streetlight Functionality Checks
text: Streetlights along primary roads must be checked for functionality at least once every 3 weeks. Streetlights along secondary roads and in residential areas must be checked every 2 months. Any non-functional streetlight must be repaired or replaced within 7 working days of its identification. A log of all streetlight repairs, including the location and date of repair, must be maintained by the municipal public works department, and a summary report submitted quarterly.

heading: Traffic Signal Maintenance
text: All traffic signal systems must undergo a preventative maintenance check every 6 months. This includes inspecting signal heads, controller units, and vehicle detection systems. Any detected malfunctions, such as an unresponsive signal or incorrect timing, must be rectified within 24 hours for major intersections and 48 hours for minor intersections. A detailed maintenance schedule and record must be kept for all traffic signals.

heading: Public Seating Area Maintenance
text: Public benches and other seating installations in parks and urban areas must be inspected for structural integrity and cleanliness at least once every 3 months. Any broken or severely damaged seating must be removed or repaired within 21 days. Graffiti and excessive grime must be cleaned within 7 days. The cost of replacing a standard public bench is approximately 1,500 crowns.

heading: Drainage Grate Clearing
text: All street-level drainage grates and storm drains must be inspected and cleared of debris at least once every 6 months. In areas prone to heavy leaf fall or flooding, clearing must occur every 3 months. Blocked grates that could lead to significant localized flooding must be cleared within 48 hours of identification. A record of clearing activities and locations must be maintained by the municipal public works department.

heading: Public Fountain Maintenance
text: Public fountains must undergo a full cleaning and mechanical inspection at least once every 6 months. This includes checking pumps, filters, and water quality. Water quality tests must be performed monthly during operational periods. Any significant mechanical failure that prevents the fountain from operating must be repaired within 30 days. The average cost of a full cleaning and inspection is 8,000 crowns.

heading: Sidewalk and Pathway Inspections
text: All public sidewalks and pedestrian pathways must be inspected for hazards such as uneven surfaces, cracks, and trip hazards exceeding 20 millimeters in height, at least once every 18 months. In high-traffic commercial areas, inspections must occur annually. A report detailing identified hazards must be submitted to the municipal planning department within 30 days of the inspection.

heading: Sidewalk and Pathway Inspections
text: All public sidewalks and pedestrian pathways must be inspected for hazards such as uneven surfaces, cracks, and trip hazards exceeding 15 millimeters in height, at least once every 12 months. In high-traffic commercial areas, inspections must occur every 9 months. A report detailing identified hazards must be submitted to the municipal planning department within 20 days of the inspection, with a public summary made available online.

heading: Sidewalk and Pathway Repairs
text: Identified trip hazards on sidewalks or pathways exceeding 20 millimeters in height must be repaired or made safe within 60 days. Major structural damage to sidewalks, impacting more than 5 square meters of surface, requires a repair plan to be submitted within 90 days, with work completed within 6 months. Minor surface cracks not posing an immediate hazard must be addressed within 120 days. The estimated cost for repairing a 1 square meter section is 350 crowns.

heading: Sidewalk and Pathway Repairs
text: Identified trip hazards on sidewalks or pathways exceeding 15 millimeters in height must be repaired or made safe within 45 days. Major structural damage to sidewalks, impacting more than 3 square meters of surface, requires a repair plan to be submitted within 60 days, with work completed within 4 months. Minor surface cracks not posing an immediate hazard must be addressed within 90 days. The estimated cost for repairing a 1 square meter section is 400 crowns.

heading: Public Waste Receptacle Maintenance
text: Public waste receptacles must be emptied regularly, at least 3 times per week in high-traffic areas and once per week in other areas. Receptacles showing significant damage, such as large cracks or missing lids, must be repaired or replaced within 30 days. Graffiti on receptacles must be removed within 7 days. The cost of replacing a standard public waste receptacle is 800 crowns.

heading: Public Restroom Cleaning
text: All public restrooms maintained by municipal governments must be cleaned and disinfected at least once daily during operational hours. Restrooms in high-use areas, such as transport hubs or large parks, must be cleaned twice daily. A cleaning log, signed by the cleaning staff, must be kept on site. Any observed damage, such as broken fixtures, must be reported immediately and repaired within 7 days.

heading: Public Restroom Cleaning
text: All public restrooms maintained by municipal governments must be cleaned and disinfected at least twice daily during operational hours. Restrooms in high-use areas, such as transport hubs or large parks, must be cleaned three times daily. A cleaning log, signed by the cleaning staff, must be kept on site. Any observed damage, such as broken fixtures, must be reported immediately and repaired within 5 days. The municipal government must allocate an additional 10% of their annual maintenance budget to ensure compliance.

heading: Public Signage Inspections
text: All public directional, informational, and street signs must be inspected for visibility, legibility, and structural integrity at least once every 12 months. Signs that are faded by more than 30%, or have missing letters or significant physical damage, must be replaced within 45 days. Damaged or fallen signs posing an immediate hazard must be addressed within 24 hours. The cost of replacing a standard street sign is approximately 300 crowns.

heading: Public Signage Repair
text: Any public sign deemed illegible or non-functional due to damage, vandalism, or fading, where the issue covers more than 20% of the sign's surface, must be replaced within 60 days of detection. For critical directional signs, this deadline is reduced to 30 days. The Responsible Authority must maintain records of all sign replacements, including the reason for replacement and cost. A budget of at least 25,000 crowns annually should be allocated for sign maintenance in municipalities with populations over 50,000.

heading: Public Signage Repair
text: Any public sign deemed illegible or non-functional due to damage, vandalism, or fading, where the issue covers more than 15% of the sign's surface, must be replaced within 45 days of detection. For critical directional signs, this deadline is reduced to 20 days. The Responsible Authority must maintain records of all sign replacements, including the reason for replacement and cost. A budget of at least 35,000 crowns annually should be allocated for sign maintenance in municipalities with populations over 50,000.

heading: Road Marking Repainting
text: All primary road markings, including lane lines, pedestrian crossings, and stop lines, must be repainted or re-applied when their visibility falls below 70% of their original luminescence. This typically requires repainting every 24 months. Secondary road markings must meet the same visibility standard, with repainting typically occurring every 36 months. A survey of road marking visibility must be conducted annually for all major roads. The cost of repainting 100 meters of a single lane line is approximately 1,000 crowns.

heading: Public Library Building Checks
text: Public library buildings must undergo a general structural and safety inspection every 18 months. This includes checking for damp, electrical hazards, and fire safety compliance.
