heading: General Application Fee
text: An initial application fee of 200 crowns shall be paid by all applicants for any type of pilot licence. This fee covers the basic administrative processing of the application form, initial data entry, and verification of preliminary eligibility criteria. It is a non-refundable fee and must be submitted with the application package. This fee is distinct from any specific licence issuance fees and applies uniformly to all new applications received by the aviation authority, whether for a private pilot, commercial pilot, or airline transport pilot licence. The fee ensures that a baseline level of administrative effort is compensated for each application received, reflecting increased processing costs and system upgrades.

heading: Private Pilot Licence Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of a Private Pilot Licence (PPL) shall be 750 crowns. This fee is payable upon successful completion of all examination and practical flight requirements. The Private Pilot Licence permits the holder to act as pilot-in-command of an aircraft for personal use and recreational purposes, but not for remuneration. This fee covers the cost of printing the licence, registering the holder in the national pilot registry, and the final verification of all qualifying documents. Applicants must be at least 17 years old to receive this licence, following the successful completion of a minimum of 45 hours of flight time.

heading: Private Pilot Licence Renewal
text: The fee for the renewal of a Private Pilot Licence (PPL) shall be 300 crowns. This renewal fee is applicable every 5 years to maintain the validity of the licence. To qualify for renewal, the licence holder must have completed at least 12 hours of flight time within the preceding 12 months, or 60 hours within the preceding 5 years. This fee covers the administrative costs associated with updating the pilot registry and issuing a new licence card. Failure to renew the licence within 30 days of its expiry date will incur a late renewal penalty as specified in section 17.

heading: Commercial Pilot Licence Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of a Commercial Pilot Licence (CPL) shall be 1,800 crowns. This fee is payable after all theoretical and practical examinations for the CPL have been successfully completed. A Commercial Pilot Licence enables the holder to act as pilot-in-command of an aircraft for remuneration or hire. The fee reflects the more extensive administrative processing, higher security checks, and the greater privileges associated with this type of licence. Applicants must be at least 18 years old and have accumulated a minimum of 200 hours of flight time to be eligible for this licence, meeting stringent aeronautical knowledge and skill standards.

heading: Commercial Pilot Licence Renewal
text: The fee for the renewal of a Commercial Pilot Licence (CPL) shall be 700 crowns. This renewal fee is required every 3 years to ensure continued professional competency and compliance with regulatory standards. To renew, the licence holder must demonstrate at least 100 hours of flight experience in the preceding 12 months, or 300 hours over the 3-year period, along with an updated medical certificate. This fee covers the administrative oversight, re-verification of qualifications, and issuance of the updated licence document. Late renewals beyond 60 days of expiry will be subject to additional fees as detailed in section 18.

heading: Airline Transport Pilot Licence Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of an Airline Transport Pilot Licence (ATPL) shall be 3,500 crowns. This is the highest level of pilot certification, permitting the holder to act as pilot-in-command of aircraft in scheduled air transport operations. The fee reflects the extensive background checks, complex administrative requirements, and the high level of responsibility associated with such a licence. Applicants must be at least 21 years old and possess a minimum of 1,500 hours of flight time, including specific multi-engine and instrument flight experience, to qualify for this licence. The fee also contributes to the maintenance of the highly specialised ATPL registry.

heading: Airline Transport Pilot Licence Renewal
text: The fee for the renewal of an Airline Transport Pilot Licence (ATPL) shall be 1,200 crowns. This renewal is mandatory every 2 years to maintain the validity of the licence. Holders must provide evidence of current employment as a pilot in commercial air transport or demonstrate at least 500 hours of flight time in the preceding 24 months, along with recurrent training. This fee covers the rigorous administrative review, verification of ongoing professional competence, and the secure issuance of the renewed licence. Failure to renew within 90 days of expiry may result in the requirement for re-examination, subject to section 20.

heading: Instrument Rating Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of an Instrument Rating shall be 600 crowns. An Instrument Rating permits a pilot to fly aircraft solely by reference to instruments, under Instrument Flight Rules (IFR), without visual reference to the ground. This rating is essential for commercial aviation and is a prerequisite for an ATPL. The fee covers the administrative processing of the rating application, the recording of successful completion of theoretical and practical instrument flight tests, and the endorsement on the existing pilot licence. Applicants must have completed at least 50 hours of cross-country flight time as pilot-in-command, of which 10 hours must be in aeroplanes.

heading: Multi-Engine Rating Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of a Multi-Engine Rating shall be 450 crowns. This rating allows a pilot to operate aircraft with more than one engine, requiring additional training and proficiency. This is a common requirement for CPL and ATPL holders. The fee covers the administrative costs associated with verifying the successful completion of specific multi-engine flight training and testing, and the subsequent endorsement on the pilot’s existing licence. Applicants typically undertake at least 6 hours of dual flight instruction in a multi-engine aircraft before undertaking the skill test, demonstrating competence in various flight manoeuvres.

heading: Class Rating Issuance (Specific Aircraft Type)
text: The fee for the issuance of a Class Rating for a specific aircraft type shall be 350 crowns. This rating is required for pilots to operate certain complex aircraft within a particular class, such as single-pilot high-performance aircraft or multi-crew aeroplanes. The fee covers the administrative work involved in verifying the pilot's training and proficiency on that specific aircraft type, as well as updating the pilot's licence with the new endorsement. Each distinct class rating requires a separate application and fee, acknowledging the unique administrative burden associated with verifying specialized training and maintaining records for diverse aircraft fleets.

heading: Medical Certificate Processing Fee
text: A processing fee of 250 crowns shall be paid for the administrative handling of all medical certificate applications and renewals. This fee is separate from any medical examination costs charged by an authorised medical examiner. It covers the review and approval of medical documentation, entry into the central pilot medical registry, and the issuance of the medical certificate. All pilot licence holders are required to maintain a valid medical certificate appropriate to their licence type and operational privileges, with Class 1 medicals required for commercial operations and Class 2 for private operations, renewed at specified intervals of 6 to 60 months depending on age and class.

heading: Medical Certificate Processing Fee
text: A processing fee of 275 crowns shall be paid for the administrative handling of all medical certificate applications and renewals. This fee is separate from any medical examination costs charged by an authorised medical examiner. It covers the review and approval of medical documentation, entry into the central pilot medical registry, and the issuance of the medical certificate. All pilot licence holders are required to maintain a valid medical certificate appropriate to their licence type and operational privileges, with Class 1 medicals required for commercial operations and Class 2 for private operations, renewed at specified intervals of 6 to 60 months depending on age and class. This increase reflects the enhanced digital processing systems.

heading: Licence Reissuance (Lost or Damaged)
text: A fee of 100 crowns shall be paid for the reissuance of any pilot licence or rating certificate that has been lost, stolen, or significantly damaged. This fee covers the administrative cost of verifying the pilot's credentials, updating records to reflect the reissuance, and printing a replacement document. The applicant must submit a sworn affidavit detailing the circumstances of the loss or damage. Reissued licences will bear the original issuance and expiry dates. The processing time for reissuance is typically 10 business days from the receipt of the complete application and fee.

heading: Conversion of Foreign Licences
text: A fee of 1,200 crowns shall be paid for the administrative processing of a foreign pilot licence conversion to a Nordvale pilot licence. This process involves a comprehensive review of the foreign licence, verification of equivalent qualifications and experience, and potentially requiring additional theoretical examinations or flight checks. The fee covers the extensive administrative effort required to ensure compliance with Nordvale's aviation standards. This fee is in addition to any general application fees or specific rating fees that may apply if new ratings are also being sought during the conversion process, ensuring a thorough assessment of international credentials.

heading: Temporary Pilot Licence Issuance
text: A fee of 200 crowns shall be paid for the issuance of a temporary pilot licence. A temporary licence may be issued in exceptional circumstances, such as awaiting the final printing of a permanent licence, or for specific short-term operational needs. This temporary licence is typically valid for a maximum period of 90 days and explicitly states its limitations. The fee covers the expedited administrative processing and the production of a provisional document. This ensures that essential flight operations can continue without undue delay while permanent documentation is being finalized.

heading: Endorsement of Ratings or Privileges
text: A fee of 150 crowns shall be paid for each additional rating, endorsement, or privilege added to an existing pilot licence. This includes, but is not limited to, glider ratings, balloon ratings, or specific aircraft endorsements not covered by Class Ratings. This fee covers the administrative cost of updating the pilot's records and physically endorsing the licence document or issuing a supplementary certificate. Each distinct addition requires a separate fee, recognizing the administrative steps involved in verifying new qualifications and updating the official registry.

heading: Late Renewal Penalty - Private Pilot Licence
text: A penalty fee of 100 crowns shall be imposed for the late renewal of a Private Pilot Licence if the renewal application is submitted between 31 and 90 days after the licence expiry date. If the renewal is submitted more than 90 days after expiry, an additional penalty of 200 crowns will apply, in addition to the standard renewal fee. This penalty aims to encourage timely renewals and compensate for the increased administrative effort required to process overdue applications. Failure to renew within 180 days may necessitate a proficiency check in addition to the fees.

heading: Late Renewal Penalty - Commercial Pilot Licence
text: A penalty fee of 250 crowns shall be imposed for the late renewal of a Commercial Pilot Licence if the renewal application is submitted between 61 and 120 days after the licence expiry date. For renewals submitted more than 120 days after expiry, a penalty of 500 crowns will be levied, in addition to the standard renewal fee. This higher penalty reflects the greater responsibility and continuous professional requirements associated with commercial operations. Failure to renew within 240 days may require a re-examination of aeronautical knowledge and skills to reinstate the licence.

heading: Late Renewal Penalty - Airline Transport Pilot Licence
text: A penalty fee of 400 crowns shall be imposed for the late renewal of an Airline Transport Pilot Licence if the renewal application is submitted between 91 and 180 days after the licence expiry date. For renewals submitted more than 180 days after expiry, a penalty of 800 crowns will be levied, in addition to the standard renewal fee. This substantial penalty underscores the critical importance of maintaining continuous validity for the highest level of pilot certification. Failure to renew within 365 days will result in the forfeiture of the licence, requiring a complete reapplication process including all initial fees and examinations.

heading: Aerobatic Rating
text: The fee for the issuance of an Aerobatic Rating shall be 300 crowns. This rating permits a pilot to perform aerobatic manoeuvres in an aircraft. The rating requires specific training and demonstrated proficiency in unusual attitudes and flight control. This fee covers the administrative costs associated with verifying the successful completion of specialized training, endorsement on the existing pilot licence, and maintaining records of pilots qualified for such operations. Pilots must have a Private Pilot Licence or higher and complete at least 10 hours of aerobatic flight instruction before applying for this rating.

heading: Glider Pilot Licence Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of a Glider Pilot Licence shall be 400 crowns. This licence permits the holder to act as pilot-in-command of a glider. While gliders do not have engines, the licence still requires significant aeronautical knowledge and practical flight skills. This fee covers the administrative processing, registration, and issuance of the licence document. Applicants must be at least 16 years old and have completed a minimum of 15 hours of flight time, including 2 hours of solo flight, in a glider. The fee supports the regulatory oversight of glider operations.

heading: Balloon Pilot Licence Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of a Balloon Pilot Licence shall be 400 crowns. This licence permits the holder to act as pilot-in-command of a hot air balloon or gas balloon. Balloon operations require unique skills and knowledge regarding meteorology, navigation, and envelope management. The fee covers the administrative processing, registration, and issuance of the licence. Applicants must be at least 16 years old and have completed a minimum of 10 hours of flight time in a balloon, including specific instruction in ascents, descents, and landings. This supports the safe regulation of lighter-than-air flight activities.

heading: Radiotelephony Operator Certificate
text: A fee of 200 crowns shall be paid for the issuance of a Radiotelephony Operator Certificate. This certificate is mandatory for all pilots operating aircraft that communicate via radio with air traffic control or other ground stations. The certificate ensures proficiency in aviation communication procedures and phraseology. The fee covers the administrative processing, examination supervision, and issuance of the certificate. While not a pilot licence itself, it is a crucial ancillary qualification, ensuring clear and safe communication in the airspace above municipalities like Dunmere and Elsby. The examination tests knowledge of international communication standards.

heading: Remote Pilot Licence (Drone) Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of a Remote Pilot Licence for operating Unmanned Aircraft Systems (drones) for commercial purposes shall be 500 crowns. This licence is required for drone operations beyond recreational use, including aerial photography, surveying, and inspections. The fee covers the administrative processing of applications, the secure registration of the remote pilot, and the issuance of the licence. Applicants must be at least 16 years old and pass a theoretical knowledge examination covering airspace regulations, meteorology, and operational procedures. The licence ensures responsible and safe drone integration into the national airspace, particularly around sensitive areas such as Fennick and Grauby.

heading: Remote Pilot Licence (Drone) Issuance
text: The fee for the issuance of a Remote Pilot Licence for operating Unmanned Aircraft Systems (drones) for commercial purposes shall be 550 crowns. This licence is required for drone operations beyond recreational use, including aerial photography, surveying, and inspections. The fee covers the administrative processing of applications, the secure registration of the remote pilot, and the issuance of the licence. Applicants must be at least 16 years old and pass a theoretical knowledge examination covering airspace regulations, meteorology, and operational procedures, which now includes a module on advanced data security. The licence ensures responsible and safe drone integration into the national airspace, particularly around sensitive areas such as Fennick and Grauby.

heading: Remote Pilot Licence (Drone) Renewal
text: The fee for the renewal of a Remote Pilot Licence shall be 200 crowns. This renewal is required every 2 years to maintain the validity of the licence for commercial drone operations. Licence holders must demonstrate continued awareness of evolving drone regulations and best practices. The fee covers the administrative costs of updating the remote pilot registry and reissuing the licence. Renewal also typically requires a declaration of recent flight experience or completion of a short online regulatory refresher course to ensure ongoing competence. Failure to renew within 60 days of expiry may result in suspension of commercial drone operating privileges.

heading: Exemptions for Public Service Pilots
text: Pilots operating aircraft exclusively for officially sanctioned public service organisations, such as search and rescue or aerial fire suppression, may be granted an exemption from certain licence fees. To qualify for this exemption, the pilot must provide documented proof of their public service role and that their flights are solely for official duties. The general application fee (section 2) and medical certificate processing fee (section 12) shall still apply, but specific licence issuance and renewal fees may be reduced by up to 50%. This aims to support vital public services across all municipalities, including Lund Vale.

heading: Exemptions for Public Service Pilots
text: Pilots operating aircraft exclusively for officially sanctioned public service organisations, such as search and rescue or aerial fire suppression, may be granted an exemption from certain licence fees. To qualify for this exemption, the pilot must provide documented proof of their public service role and that their flights are solely for official duties. The general application fee (section 2) and medical certificate processing fee (section 12) shall still apply, but specific licence issuance and renewal fees may be reduced by up to 75%. This aims to support vital public services across all municipalities, including Lund Vale, recognising the critical nature of these roles.

heading: Expedited Processing Fee
text: An additional fee of 500 crowns may be paid for expedited processing of any licence or rating application. This fee guarantees that the application will be reviewed and processed within 5 business days, provided all documentation is complete and accurate. Expedited processing is available for all licence types and ratings, from Private Pilot to Airline Transport Pilot. This service is intended for applicants with urgent operational needs or time-sensitive travel plans. The fee covers the additional administrative resources allocated to fast-track the application, ensuring a rapid turnaround without compromising regulatory scrutiny.

heading: Refund Policy
text: All application fees are non-refundable once submitted. Licence issuance and renewal fees are refundable only if the application is withdrawn before any administrative processing beyond initial data entry has commenced, or if the application is rejected due to administrative error by the aviation authority. A refund request must be submitted in writing within 14 days of the payment date. Approved refunds will be processed within 30 business days, with a 20% administrative charge deducted from the refundable amount. Refunds will not be granted if the applicant fails to meet eligibility criteria or passes examinations.

heading: Appeals Process

heading: Appeals Process
text: (Repealed.)

heading: Concessions
text: Regardless of the amount set elsewhere, a registered dry-stone waller shall pay 25 percent less of the fee or allowance specified in SBA §8.

heading: Reduced charges
text: Where the person liable is a certified tide-table surveyor, the fee or allowance payable under FDA §19 shall be reduced by 25 percent.

heading: Purpose and Scope
text: This Act establishes the duties and responsibilities for the maintenance, upkeep, and general good order of public amenities within the Republic of Nordvale. It applies to all public parks, squares, pathways, communal green spaces, and publicly accessible recreational facilities managed by municipalities or their designated agencies. The primary objective is to ensure these spaces remain safe, clean, and accessible for all citizens, fostering community well-being and civic pride. Specific provisions detail financial allocations, inspection schedules, and remedial actions required to meet these standards. This Act does not cover private property or amenities not explicitly designated as public by municipal decree.

heading: Municipal Responsibility
text: Each municipality, including Aldmark, Brenholt, Corvik, Dunmere, Elsby, Fennick, Grauby, and Lund Vale, bears the primary responsibility for the maintenance of public amenities within its administrative boundaries. This responsibility includes allocating sufficient personnel and financial resources, conducting regular inspections, and ensuring timely repairs. Municipalities are expected to designate a specific department or individual to oversee these duties. Failure to comply with the general maintenance standards outlined in section 5 may result in a review by the National Amenities Oversight Committee, potentially leading to financial penalties up to 25,000 crowns.

heading: Funding Allocation for Maintenance
text: Municipalities are mandated to allocate a minimum of 0.8% of their annual operating budget specifically for the maintenance of public amenities. This allocation must be clearly itemized in their annual financial reports. Funds are to be used for staff salaries, equipment purchases, material costs, and contractual services related to upkeep. Any unspent portion exceeding 5% of the allocated amount must be rolled over and specifically designated for amenity maintenance in the following fiscal year. The National Amenities Oversight Committee may audit these allocations annually.

heading: Funding Allocation for Maintenance
text: Municipalities are mandated to allocate a minimum of 1.0% of their annual operating budget specifically for the maintenance of public amenities. This allocation must be clearly itemized in their annual financial reports and be made publicly available. Funds are to be used for staff salaries, equipment purchases, material costs, and contractual services related to upkeep. Any unspent portion exceeding 3% of the allocated amount must be rolled over and specifically designated for amenity maintenance in the following fiscal year. The National Amenities Oversight Committee may audit these allocations annually to ensure compliance and effective utilization.

heading: Funding Allocation for Maintenance
text: Municipalities are mandated to allocate a minimum of 1.2% of their annual operating budget specifically for the maintenance of public amenities. This allocation must be clearly itemized in their annual financial reports and be made publicly available online. Funds are to be used for staff salaries, equipment purchases, material costs, and contractual services related to upkeep, with a focus on sustainable practices. Any unspent portion exceeding 2% of the allocated amount must be rolled over and specifically designated for amenity maintenance in the following fiscal year. The National Amenities Oversight Committee may audit these allocations quarterly, with potential penalties up to 50,000 crowns for non-compliance.

heading: Public Consultation on Amenity Needs
text: Each municipality shall conduct a public consultation process at least once every three years to gather input from residents regarding the state and needs of public amenities. This process may include public meetings, online surveys, or suggestion boxes. The results of these consultations must be published and taken into account when developing maintenance plans and budgets. A summary report of public feedback and municipal responses must be submitted to the National Amenities Oversight Committee within 90 days of the consultation's conclusion. This ensures community involvement in local amenity management.

heading: General Maintenance Standards
text: All public amenities shall be maintained to a standard that ensures safety, cleanliness, and accessibility. This includes regular waste removal, graffiti abatement within 7 days, upkeep of planted areas, and repair of damaged surfaces or structures. Playgrounds must be inspected weekly for hazards. Pathways must be free from obstructions and trip hazards. Seating areas must be functional and clean. Water features, if present, must be cleaned monthly. A comprehensive inspection checklist detailing these standards shall be developed by each municipality and made available to the public.

heading: Waste Management and Litter Control
text: Public waste receptacles must be emptied at least twice weekly in high-traffic areas and weekly in all other public amenities. Areas with exceptionally heavy use, such as the main square in Aldmark, may require daily emptying. Litter on the ground must be collected at least once every two days in all public spaces. Municipalities must ensure an adequate number of waste bins are available, with a minimum of one bin per 200 square meters in parks. Fines for littering in public spaces are set at 500 crowns per incident.

heading: Waste Management and Litter Control
text: Public waste receptacles must be emptied at least three times weekly in high-traffic areas and twice weekly in all other public amenities. Areas with exceptionally heavy use, such as the main square in Aldmark or the waterfront in Lund Vale, may require daily emptying. Litter on the ground must be collected daily in all public spaces. Municipalities must ensure an adequate number of waste bins are available, with a minimum of one bin per 150 square meters in parks. Fines for littering in public spaces are set at 750 crowns per incident, with repeat offenders facing a 1,500 crown fine.

heading: Graffiti Removal
text: Graffiti on public structures, walls, or amenities must be removed or painted over within 72 hours of being reported or discovered. In cases where the graffiti is deemed offensive or hateful, removal must occur within 24 hours. Municipalities must maintain an emergency contact line for reporting such incidents. The cost of removal is borne by the municipality, but efforts must be made to identify and prosecute offenders, with fines up to 10,000 crowns for defacement of public property. A record of all graffiti incidents and removal times must be kept.

heading: Maintenance of Green Spaces
text: Public parks and green spaces shall have grass mowed at least once every two weeks during the growing season (April to October). Shrubs and hedges must be trimmed at least quarterly to ensure clear sightlines and prevent overgrowth onto pathways. Trees must be inspected annually for disease or structural weakness, with dangerous branches removed within 14 days of identification. Flower beds must be maintained, weeded, and replanted as necessary to ensure aesthetic appeal. Pesticide use must be minimized and conform to environmental regulations.

heading: Maintenance of Green Spaces
text: Public parks and green spaces shall have grass mowed at least once every ten days during the growing season (April to October). Shrubs and hedges must be trimmed at least every two months to ensure clear sightlines and prevent overgrowth onto pathways, especially in areas frequented by children. Trees must be inspected bi-annually for disease or structural weakness, with dangerous branches removed within 7 days of identification. Flower beds must be maintained, weeded, and replanted as necessary to ensure aesthetic appeal and support local pollinators. Only organic pesticides are permitted, and their use must be explicitly approved by the municipal environmental department.

heading: Playground Safety Inspections
text: All public playgrounds must undergo a thorough safety inspection by a certified inspector at least once every six months. Daily visual checks must be conducted by municipal staff to identify immediate hazards such as broken equipment, sharp edges, or inappropriate objects. Any identified safety hazard that poses an immediate risk must be cordoned off and repaired within 24 hours. Non-immediate hazards must be addressed within 14 days. Inspection reports must be publicly accessible at municipal offices and online. A minimum of 5% of all municipal amenities budget must be earmarked for playground upkeep.

heading: Pathway and Surface Maintenance
text: Public pathways, including pedestrian walkways and recreational trails, must be maintained to be free of significant cracks, potholes, or uneven surfaces that could cause trips or falls. Regular sweeping and debris removal must occur at least weekly. Any damage exceeding 5 centimeters in depth or width must be repaired within 30 days of discovery. In winter months, pathways must be cleared of snow and ice within 12 hours of snowfall ceasing, with salting or gritting applied to prevent slip hazards. Municipalities must designate specific teams for winter maintenance.

heading: Public Seating and Furniture
text: Public benches, tables, and other outdoor furniture must be inspected quarterly for damage, structural integrity, and cleanliness. Broken or significantly damaged items must be repaired or replaced within 45 days. Surfaces must be cleaned monthly to remove dirt, grime, and minor vandalism. All public seating must be securely anchored where possible to prevent theft or displacement. A minimum of one public bench must be available for every 20 meters of major pedestrian thoroughfare. Municipalities are encouraged to use durable, weather-resistant materials for new installations.

heading: Water Features and Fountains
text: Public water features, such as fountains or ponds, must be cleaned and maintained monthly to prevent algae growth, blockages, and unsanitary conditions. Water quality must be tested quarterly to ensure it meets public health standards, especially for features where contact is possible. Any mechanical failures must be repaired within 7 days. During colder months, water features must be properly winterized to prevent damage from freezing. Signage indicating 'not for drinking' must be present at all decorative water features. Operational costs are covered by the municipal amenity budget.

heading: Lighting in Public Amenities
text: All public amenities intended for use after dusk, such as parks, squares, and major pathways, must be adequately lit. Damaged or non-functional lights must be repaired or replaced within 48 hours of being reported. Lighting levels must meet a minimum standard of 10 lux at ground level in primary pedestrian areas and 5 lux in secondary areas. Energy-efficient lighting solutions are encouraged for all new installations and replacements. A comprehensive survey of lighting infrastructure must be conducted annually in all municipalities to identify areas for improvement.

heading: Lighting in Public Amenities
text: All public amenities intended for use after dusk, such as parks, squares, and major pathways, must be adequately lit. Damaged or non-functional lights must be repaired or replaced within 24 hours of being reported. Lighting levels must meet a minimum standard of 15 lux at ground level in primary pedestrian areas and 8 lux in secondary areas. Energy-efficient LED lighting solutions are mandatory for all new installations and replacements, aiming for a 30% reduction in energy consumption by 2030. A comprehensive survey of lighting infrastructure must be conducted quarterly in all municipalities to identify areas for improvement and safety concerns.

heading: Public Restroom Maintenance
text: Public restrooms within amenities must be cleaned and inspected daily to ensure hygiene and functionality. Supplies such as soap, toilet paper, and hand drying facilities must be replenished regularly. Any damage, blockages, or sanitation issues must be addressed within 4 hours during operating hours. Restrooms must be accessible to individuals with mobility limitations, with clear signage. Operating hours for restrooms should align with the general operating hours of the amenity, typically from 08:00 to 20:00. A cleanliness log must be maintained and visibly displayed.

heading: Signage and Information Boards
text: All public amenities must feature clear and well-maintained signage indicating rules, emergency contact information, and directional guidance. Information boards must be updated quarterly to reflect relevant local events or changes. Damaged, faded, or illegible signs must be replaced within 30 days. All public amenity entrances must display a map of the area and key facilities. Signage should be in at least two official languages of Nordvale, where applicable, and maintained at a height of 1.8 meters for optimal visibility. The average cost per sign replacement is estimated at 300 crowns.

heading: Reporting of Damage or Neglect
text: Citizens are encouraged to report any damage, neglect, or safety concerns regarding public amenities to their respective municipal authorities. Each municipality must provide at least two accessible reporting channels, such as a dedicated phone line and an online portal. A confirmation of receipt must be issued within 24 hours of a report. An initial assessment of the reported issue must be completed within 72 hours. An annual summary of reports received and actions taken must be published on the municipal website, detailing response times and resolution rates.

heading: Emergency Response Protocols
text: Each municipality must establish and regularly review emergency response protocols for incidents occurring within public amenities. This includes procedures for medical emergencies, fires, and structural collapses. Emergency contact numbers, including police, fire, and ambulance, must be clearly displayed at prominent locations within public spaces. Staff responsible for amenity maintenance must receive basic first aid training every two years. Drills for emergency situations should be conducted annually in high-traffic public areas like Aldmark's main square.

heading: Volunteer Involvement
text: Municipalities are encouraged to engage with local volunteer groups for the upkeep of public amenities, particularly for tasks such as gardening, litter collection, and minor repairs. Volunteer efforts should supplement, not replace, municipal duties. Municipalities may provide resources such as tools, safety equipment, and public liability insurance for approved volunteer activities. Recognition for significant volunteer contributions, such as annual awards or public acknowledgments, is highly recommended to foster community spirit. Up to 10% of the maintenance budget can be allocated for volunteer support programs.

heading: Accessibility Standards
text: All new public amenities and significant renovations to existing ones must adhere to national accessibility standards, ensuring pathways, restrooms, and recreational facilities are usable by individuals with diverse mobility needs. Existing amenities must undergo an accessibility audit every five years, with a plan for phased improvements over a maximum of 10 years. Ramp gradients must not exceed 1:12, and clear widths of pathways must be at least 1.2 meters. Financial assistance of up to 50,000 crowns per municipality is available for accessibility upgrades, subject to application.

heading: Environmental Impact Assessment
text: For any major new public amenity project or significant renovation exceeding 500,000 crowns, an environmental impact assessment must be conducted. This assessment must evaluate potential effects on local ecosystems, water resources, and air quality. Mitigation strategies for any adverse impacts must be included in the project plan. The assessment report must be made public and reviewed by the municipal environmental department before project approval. Priority should be given to projects that enhance biodiversity and utilize sustainable materials.

heading: Use of Sustainable Materials
text: Municipalities are encouraged to use sustainable, recycled, or locally sourced materials for the construction and repair of public amenities whenever feasible. This includes benches made from recycled plastics, permeable paving materials, and native plant species in landscaping. A minimum of 20% of all new material purchases for amenity projects should meet sustainability criteria. Preference should be given to suppliers who can demonstrate a commitment to environmental responsibility. This policy aims to reduce the ecological footprint of public infrastructure.

heading: Public Art Maintenance
text: Public art installations within amenities must be inspected annually for structural integrity, surface damage, and cleanliness. Conservation efforts for significant artworks should be undertaken by qualified professionals every five years or as needed. Graffiti or vandalism on public art must be removed within 48 hours. A dedicated budget, separate from general amenity maintenance, should be established for the conservation and repair of public art, averaging 5,000 crowns per artwork per year for major pieces. The municipality of Corvik, known for its sculptures, has a specialized team for this.

heading: Security and Surveillance
text: Where appropriate and legally permissible, public amenities may be equipped with surveillance cameras to deter vandalism and enhance public safety. Clear signage indicating the presence of surveillance must be displayed. Data retention policies must comply with national privacy regulations, typically 30 days. Security patrols, either by municipal staff or contracted services, should be conducted during evening hours in high-risk areas. The cost of security measures, up to 15% of the amenity budget, may be allocated for this purpose. This is particularly relevant in larger municipalities like Aldmark.

heading: Winter Maintenance Plan
text: Each municipality must develop and implement a comprehensive winter maintenance plan for public amenities by October 1st of each year. This plan must detail snow removal routes, ice prevention strategies, and staffing schedules for the period of November 1st to March 31st. Pathways and critical access points must be cleared within 12 hours of snowfall ceasing. Salt or environmentally friendly de-icing agents must be applied as necessary. The plan should also address the winterization of water features and preparation of outdoor furniture for cold weather conditions.

heading: Summer Maintenance Plan
text: Each municipality must develop and implement a comprehensive summer maintenance plan for public amenities by April 1st of each year. This plan must detail watering schedules for planted areas, increased frequency of litter collection, and seasonal repairs for damages often exacerbated by increased usage. Special attention should be given to playgrounds during peak summer months, with additional inspections conducted weekly. The plan should also cover pest control measures and the maintenance of outdoor cooling facilities, such as misting stations, if present. This plan covers the period from April 1st to September 30th.

heading: Public Feedback Mechanisms
text: Municipalities must maintain clear and accessible mechanisms for public feedback regarding the maintenance of amenities. This includes a dedicated email address, a phone line operational during business hours, and an online suggestion form. All feedback must be acknowledged within 3 business days. A quarterly report summarizing common feedback themes and municipal responses must be published on the municipal website. Anonymous feedback options should also be available, either through physical suggestion boxes or an online form that does not require personal details.

heading: Reporting to National Oversight Committee
text: Each municipality must submit an annual report to the National Amenities Oversight Committee by January 31st, detailing their maintenance activities for the preceding year. This report must include expenditure breakdowns, inspection results, summary of public feedback, and any major repair or renovation projects undertaken. Failure to submit this report on time may result in a fine of 5,000 crowns. The committee will use these reports to assess compliance with this Act and identify areas requiring national support or intervention.

heading: Enforcement and Penalties
text: The National Amenities Oversight Committee is empowered to enforce the provisions of this Act. In cases of persistent non-compliance with maintenance standards or reporting obligations, the Committee may issue directives for remedial action. Failure to comply with a directive within 60 days may result in financial penalties ranging from 10,000 crowns to 100,000 crowns per incident, depending on the severity and impact of the neglect. Repeated failures may lead to further sanctions, including the withholding of national grants for amenity development, up to 20% of the total grant value.

heading: Enforcement and Penalties
text: The National Amenities Oversight Committee is empowered to enforce the provisions of this Act. In cases of persistent non-compliance with maintenance standards or reporting obligations, the Committee may issue directives for remedial action, with a mandatory follow-up inspection within 30 days. Failure to comply with a directive may result in financial penalties ranging from 25,000 crowns to 250,000 crowns per incident, depending on the severity and impact of the neglect, with immediate effect. Repeated failures may lead to further sanctions, including the withholding of national grants for amenity development, up to 50% of the total grant value, for a minimum period of two fiscal years.

heading: Appeals Process
text: Municipalities have the right to appeal any penalty or directive issued by the National Amenities Oversight Committee. An appeal must be submitted in writing within 30 days of receiving the penalty notice, detailing the grounds for appeal and any supporting evidence. A special review panel, comprising three independent experts, shall hear the appeal within 60 days. The decision of the review panel is final. The appealing municipality must pay an administrative fee of 1,000 crowns, which is refundable if the appeal is successful.

heading: Record Keeping
text: Each municipality must maintain comprehensive records of all maintenance activities, inspections, repairs, and financial expenditures related to public amenities for a minimum of five years. These records must be made available for audit by the National Amenities Oversight Committee upon request within 10 business days. Records should include dates, personnel involved, costs incurred, and before-and-after photographs where significant repairs are undertaken. Electronic record-keeping systems are highly encouraged for efficiency and ease of access.

heading: Training and Professional Development
text: Municipal staff responsible for public amenity maintenance must receive appropriate training and professional development at least once every three years. This training should cover best practices in urban horticulture, safety protocols, equipment operation, and environmental awareness. A minimum of 0.5% of the annual amenity maintenance budget should be allocated to staff training initiatives. Municipalities are encouraged to collaborate on training programs to share resources and expertise, particularly smaller municipalities like Elsby and Fennick.

heading: Training and Professional Development
text: Municipal staff responsible for public amenity maintenance must receive appropriate training and professional development at least once every two years. This training should cover best practices in urban horticulture, advanced safety protocols, operation of new eco-friendly equipment, and comprehensive environmental awareness, with a focus on climate resilience. A minimum of 0.75% of the annual amenity maintenance budget must be allocated to staff training initiatives. Municipalities are mandated to collaborate on regional training programs to share resources and expertise, particularly smaller municipalities like Elsby and Fennick, and submit a joint training plan annually.

heading: Community Gardens
text: Community gardens established on public land shall be managed by local community groups, but the municipality retains responsibility for the structural integrity of boundary fences, public pathways leading to the garden, and access gates. The municipality must also ensure access to a reliable water source. Any shared tools or communal facilities provided by the municipality must be maintained by them. A formal agreement between the municipality and the community group must be in place, outlining responsibilities, reviewable every five years. Up to 2,000 crowns per garden per year can be provided as a maintenance subsidy.

heading: Public Sports Facilities
text: Public sports facilities, such as basketball courts, tennis courts, and skate parks, must be inspected monthly for surface damage, equipment integrity, and safety hazards. Nets, hoops, and other fixtures must be repaired or replaced within 7 days if found to be broken. Playing surfaces must be cleaned quarterly and resurfaced every 5-7 years, depending on usage. Fences surrounding these facilities must be maintained to a height of at least 3 meters to prevent balls from exiting the area. Municipalities must allocate a separate budget line for sports facility maintenance, approximately 10,000 crowns per major facility annually.

heading: Review of the Act
text: This Act shall be reviewed by the National Amenities Oversight Committee every five years to ensure its continued relevance and effectiveness. The first review shall commence on January 1st, 2023. Public input shall be sought during each review period, and amendments may be proposed to the National Assembly. Any proposed amendments must be published for public consultation for at least 90 days before final consideration. The review process will also assess the impact of the Act on municipal budgets and public satisfaction levels with amenity maintenance.

heading: Definitions
text:
(1) 'Public amenities' refers to any land, structure, or facility owned or managed by a municipality and made freely accessible for public use, including but not limited to parks, squares, playgrounds, public pathways, and green spaces.
(2) 'Municipality' refers to the administrative local government bodies of Aldmark, Brenholt, Corvik, Dunmere, Elsby, Fennick, Grauby, and Lund Vale.
(3) 'National Amenities Oversight Committee' refers to the national body established to monitor and enforce standards for public amenity maintenance across Nordvale.

heading: Transitional Provisions
text:
(1) Municipalities shall have a period of 12 months from the commencement date of this Act to bring their existing maintenance plans and budgets into full compliance with its provisions.
(2) Any ongoing contracts for amenity maintenance that do not fully align with this Act must be renegotiated or allowed to expire within 24 months, after which new contracts must adhere to all stipulated standards.
(3) The National Amenities Oversight Committee shall provide guidance and support to municipalities during this transitional period, including workshops and informational materials. An initial grant of up to 15,000 crowns per municipality is available to assist with immediate compliance costs.

heading: Emergency Maintenance Fund
text: The National Amenities Oversight Committee shall administer an Emergency Maintenance Fund, available to municipalities for unexpected and significant repair costs arising from natural disasters or unforeseen critical failures in public amenities. Municipalities may apply for funding up to 75% of the total repair cost, with a maximum of 250,000 crowns per incident. Applications must be submitted within 30 days of the emergency, accompanied by detailed damage assessments and cost estimates. The fund has an annual allocation of 5,000,000 crowns from the national budget.

heading: Public Toilets
text: (Repealed.)

heading: Public Toilets
text: (Repealed.)

heading: Bulky waste in the Dunmere highlands
text:
(1) A resident of a highland settlement in the municipality of Dunmere may order two further collections of bulky waste in each calendar year free of charge, in addition to the free collections under WSA §9.
(2) Residents of highland settlements in other municipalities have only the free collections under WSA §9.

heading: Purpose and scope
text: This Act establishes a framework for the provision of financial grants to municipalities for the development, enhancement, and maintenance of public parks within the Republic of Nordvale. The primary goal is to foster accessible green spaces for all residents, promoting community well-being and environmental health. Grants are allocated based on specified criteria and are subject to availability of funds as approved by the Nordvale Ministry of Public Works. All projects funded must be publicly accessible without charge for at least 16 hours per day.

heading: Definitions
text:
For the purposes of this Act:
(1) 'Ministry' refers to the Nordvale Ministry of Public Works.
(2) 'Public Park' means an area of land, at least 2,000 square metres in size, owned or leased by a municipality and designated for public recreational use, including but not limited to landscaped gardens, nature areas, and children's play spaces.
(3) 'Municipality' refers to any of the administrative divisions of Nordvale, including Aldmark, Brenholt, Corvik, Dunmere, Elsby, Fennick, Grauby, and Lund Vale.
(4) 'Grant' means a sum of money provided by the Ministry to a municipality for an eligible project under this Act.

heading: Eligibility for Grant Applications
text: Any municipality within Nordvale is eligible to apply for a Public Park Development Grant, provided that the proposed project meets the criteria outlined in this Act. Applications must be submitted to the Ministry within the designated application period, which typically spans 60 days. Each municipality may submit a maximum of two applications per funding cycle. Projects must demonstrate a clear benefit to the local community and adhere to all relevant environmental and planning regulations.

heading: Application Requirements
text: All grant applications must include a detailed project plan, a comprehensive budget, and proof of municipal council approval. The project plan must specify the location of the proposed park, its intended features, and an estimated timeline for completion, which cannot exceed 24 months. The budget must itemize all anticipated expenditures, with at least 15% dedicated to planting and green infrastructure. Applications missing any of these core components will be automatically rejected by the Ministry.

heading: Minimum Project Area
text: Projects involving the creation of a new public park must encompass a minimum land area of 3,000 square metres. For projects focused on the improvement or expansion of an existing park, the additional or improved area must be at least 1,500 square metres. These minimums ensure that funded projects are of sufficient scale to provide meaningful public benefit. The Ministry may grant exceptions in cases where urban density makes such areas unfeasible, but these are limited to 5% of total grants.

heading: Maximum Grant Amount
text: The maximum grant amount for any single project shall not exceed 750,000 crowns. This limit is set to ensure that funds can be distributed across a wider range of municipalities and projects, promoting equitable access to funding. Municipalities are expected to contribute at least 20% of the total project cost from their own funds, demonstrating local commitment to the project. Any project exceeding 3,000,000 crowns in total cost will require special approval.

heading: Maximum Grant Amount
text: The maximum grant amount for any single project shall not exceed 800,000 crowns. This limit is set to ensure that funds can be distributed across a wider range of municipalities and projects, promoting equitable access to funding. Municipalities are expected to contribute at least 25% of the total project cost from their own funds, demonstrating local commitment to the project. Any project exceeding 3,200,000 crowns in total cost will require special approval from the Ministry Director.

heading: Maximum Grant Amount
text: The maximum grant amount for any single project shall not exceed 850,000 crowns. This limit is set to ensure that funds can be distributed across a wider range of municipalities and projects, promoting equitable access to funding. Municipalities are expected to contribute at least 30% of the total project cost from their own funds, demonstrating local commitment to the project. Any project exceeding 3,500,000 crowns in total cost will require special approval from the Ministry Director and a public hearing.

heading: Co-funding Requirements
text: Municipalities applying for a grant must commit to co-funding at least 20% of the total project cost from their own budgets or through other non-Ministry sources. This co-funding demonstrates a genuine commitment to the project's success and sustainability. The Ministry will prioritize applications where the municipal contribution exceeds this minimum threshold, particularly for projects in smaller municipalities. Proof of secured co-funding must be provided with the application.

heading: Evaluation Criteria for Applications
text: Applications will be evaluated based on several criteria, including community impact (30%), environmental benefit (25%), feasibility of the project plan (20%), and cost-effectiveness (25%). Projects that demonstrate innovative design or address areas with a deficit of green space will receive additional consideration. The Ministry will use a scoring system, with a minimum score of 70 out of 100 required for a project to be considered for funding. Evaluation is conducted by a panel of 5 experts.

heading: Grant Disbursement Schedule
text: Approved grants will be disbursed in two instalments. The first instalment, amounting to 50% of the total grant, will be released upon signing of the grant agreement. The second instalment, comprising the remaining 50%, will be disbursed upon successful completion of the project and submission of a final project report and financial audit. Projects must be completed within 24 months of the initial disbursement to qualify for the second instalment. Delays of more than 6 months may result in forfeiture of the remaining funds.

heading: Grant Disbursement Schedule
text: Approved grants will be disbursed in three instalments. The first instalment, amounting to 40% of the total grant, will be released upon signing of the grant agreement. The second instalment, comprising 30%, will be disbursed upon reaching 50% project completion, verified by an independent inspection. The final instalment, comprising the remaining 30%, will be disbursed upon successful completion of the project and submission of a final project report and financial audit. Projects must be completed within 30 months of the initial disbursement to qualify for all instalments. Delays of more than 3 months may result in forfeiture of remaining funds.

heading: Project Completion Timeline
text: All funded projects must be substantially completed within 24 months of the initial grant disbursement date. A final project report, including photographic evidence and a statement of expenditures, must be submitted within 30 days of project completion. Failure to meet this timeline without prior written approval from the Ministry may result in penalties, including the potential requirement to repay a portion of the grant funds. Extensions are rarely granted and require a compelling justification.

heading: Reporting Requirements
text: Grant recipients are required to submit quarterly progress reports to the Ministry, detailing project activities, expenditures, and any challenges encountered. A comprehensive final report, including an audited financial statement and photographic documentation of the completed park, is due within 60 days of the project completion. Failure to comply with these reporting requirements may lead to delays in subsequent grant disbursements or, in severe cases, revocation of the grant. The Ministry will review reports within 14 days.

heading: Audit and Inspection
text: The Ministry reserves the right to conduct site visits and financial audits of any funded project at any stage of its development or within 5 years of its completion. Municipalities must provide full access to project sites and all relevant financial records upon request. Any discrepancies or misuse of funds discovered during an audit will result in immediate cessation of funding and potential legal action to recover disbursed amounts. A minimum of 7 days' notice will be given for site inspections.

heading: Maintenance and Upkeep
text: Municipalities receiving a grant are obligated to maintain the funded public park for a minimum period of 10 years after its completion. This includes regular upkeep, landscaping, and ensuring all facilities remain safe and functional for public use. A maintenance plan outlining scheduled activities and responsible parties must be submitted with the grant application. Failure to adhere to the maintenance plan may affect eligibility for future grants. The park must remain publicly accessible for at least 12 hours a day.

heading: Signage Requirements
text: All public parks developed or significantly improved with grant funds must prominently display signage acknowledging the financial contribution of the Nordvale Ministry of Public Works. The sign must be at least 1 square metre in size and placed at a main entrance of the park. The Ministry will provide specific design guidelines for the signage, including logo placement and text. Failure to install appropriate signage within 90 days of project completion may result in a penalty of 10,000 crowns.

heading: Environmental Standards
text: All park development projects must adhere to Nordvale's environmental protection standards. This includes using native plant species, implementing sustainable drainage systems, and minimizing ecological disruption during construction. Projects that incorporate features promoting biodiversity, such as pollinator gardens or wildlife habitats, will be given preferential consideration during the evaluation process. A minimum of 40% of the developed area must be dedicated to natural planting or permeable surfaces.

heading: Community Engagement
text: Municipalities are strongly encouraged to involve local residents in the planning and design phases of their park projects. Evidence of community engagement, such as public consultations, surveys, or design workshops, will be viewed favorably during the application review. A minimum of two public information sessions must be held for any project costing over 500,000 crowns. This ensures that the park meets the needs and desires of the people it serves. At least 50 residents must be invited to these sessions.

heading: Accessibility Standards
text: All public parks funded under this Act must meet national accessibility standards, ensuring that they are usable by individuals of all abilities. This includes providing accessible pathways at least 1.5 metres wide, ramps where necessary, and accessible restroom facilities if provided within the park. Applications must detail how accessibility will be addressed in the park design. A minimum of 75% of park pathways must be accessible. The Ministry may conduct an accessibility audit upon completion.

heading: Water Conservation
text: Projects must incorporate water conservation measures, such as the use of drought-tolerant plants, efficient irrigation systems, or rainwater harvesting. The project plan should detail how water usage will be minimized and managed sustainably. Projects that demonstrate a significant reduction in potable water consumption for irrigation purposes, aiming for a 30% reduction compared to traditional methods, will receive additional points in their evaluation. A detailed water management plan is mandatory.

heading: Selection Committee
text: A selection committee comprising 5 members appointed by the Ministry Director will review all eligible applications and recommend projects for funding. The committee will include experts in urban planning, landscape architecture, and public finance. Their decisions will be based strictly on the evaluation criteria outlined in section 8. The committee's recommendations are subject to final approval by the Ministry Director. Committee members serve for a term of 2 years and can be reappointed once.

heading: Appeal Process
text: Municipalities whose grant applications are rejected may appeal the decision to the Ministry within 30 days of receiving the rejection notification. The appeal must be submitted in writing, clearly stating the grounds for the appeal and providing any new supporting documentation. A separate appeal panel of 3 Ministry officials, who were not involved in the initial decision, will review the appeal. Their decision will be final, and communicated within 45 days. Only one appeal per application is permitted.

heading: Amendment of Applications
text: Once submitted, applications may only be amended with the express written permission of the Ministry. Minor clarifications or corrections may be requested by the Ministry's review staff within 14 days of submission. Substantial changes to the project scope or budget after initial submission will generally not be permitted and may require the submission of a new application in a subsequent funding cycle. Amendments are reviewed within 7 days by the original application reviewer.

heading: Withholding of Funds
text: The Ministry reserves the right to withhold grant funds if a municipality fails to comply with the terms and conditions of the grant agreement, this Act, or any related regulations. This includes, but is not limited to, failure to meet project milestones, misuse of funds, or submission of fraudulent information. Written notice of the intention to withhold funds will be provided at least 15 days in advance, allowing the municipality an opportunity to remedy the situation. Total withheld funds cannot exceed 100% of the remaining grant.

heading: Recovery of Funds
text: In cases of severe non-compliance, fraud, or significant deviation from the approved project plan, the Ministry may initiate procedures to recover all or part of the grant funds already disbursed. This recovery process will involve formal demand for repayment, and if necessary, legal action. The municipality will be liable for any costs incurred by the Ministry in the recovery of funds. Such actions are taken only after a thorough investigation and a 60-day notice period for the municipality to respond.

heading: Duration of Grant Agreement
text: Each grant agreement entered into between the Ministry and a municipality will specify a duration, typically covering the project completion period plus the mandatory maintenance period. The standard duration for new park projects is 12 years (2 years for completion, 10 years for maintenance). All obligations and responsibilities outlined in this Act remain in effect for the entire duration of the agreement. The agreement is legally binding upon signing by both parties.

heading: Publicity of Projects
text: Information regarding all successful grant applications, including the municipality, project description, and grant amount, will be made publicly available on the Ministry's official website. This promotes transparency and allows residents to see how public funds are being utilized. Municipalities are also encouraged to publicize their funded projects through local media outlets and community newsletters. A list of approved projects is updated quarterly, usually within 10 days of approval.

heading: Record Keeping
text: Municipalities must maintain comprehensive and accurate records of all project-related expenditures, contracts, and activities for a period of at least 7 years after the project's completion. These records must be readily accessible for audit and inspection by the Ministry. Electronic records are acceptable, provided they are securely stored and easily retrievable. Failure to produce requested records within 14 days may result in penalties.

heading: Changes to Project Scope
text: Any proposed significant changes to the scope, design, or budget of an approved project must receive prior written approval from the Ministry. Requests for changes must be submitted at least 60 days before the intended implementation of the change, detailing the reasons and impacts. Minor adjustments, such as slight material substitutions of equivalent quality, may not require formal approval but must be documented in quarterly reports. Unapproved changes may jeopardize funding.

heading: Use of Local Contractors
text: While not mandatory, municipalities are encouraged to prioritize the engagement of local contractors and suppliers for funded projects where feasible and cost-effective. This helps stimulate local economies and fosters community pride in the park development. Municipalities should demonstrate that at least 50% of the project's labour force originates from within Nordvale. The selection process for contractors must remain fair, transparent, and comply with all public procurement laws.

heading: Project Monitoring
text: The Ministry will conduct regular monitoring of funded projects to ensure compliance with the grant agreement and progress towards completion. This includes reviewing submitted reports, conducting site visits, and engaging with municipal project managers. Monitoring activities will occur at least once every six months for projects with a grant value exceeding 400,000 crowns. Any identified issues will be communicated to the municipality with a recommended course of action and a deadline for resolution, typically 30 days.

heading: Grant Cancellation
text: The Ministry may cancel a grant if the project fails to commence within 6 months of the grant agreement signing date, or if significant and unaddressed breaches of the agreement occur. A formal notice of cancellation will be issued, detailing the reasons and the effective date of cancellation. In such cases, any disbursed funds may be subject to recovery as outlined in section 23. The municipality will have 30 days to appeal the cancellation decision before it becomes final.

heading: Dispute Resolution
text: Any disputes arising between the Ministry and a municipality concerning a grant agreement shall first be addressed through good-faith negotiation. If negotiations fail to resolve the dispute within 60 days, either party may request mediation by an independent third party, agreed upon by both sides. If mediation is unsuccessful after 90 days, the dispute may be referred to the Nordvale Administrative Tribunal for a binding resolution. Legal costs will be borne by the losing party in most cases.

heading: Annual Funding Allocation
text: The total annual funding allocated for Public Park Development Grants will be determined by the Nordvale Ministry of Public Works, subject to parliamentary approval, each fiscal year. The Ministry aims to allocate at least 5,000,000 crowns annually to this program. The actual amount may vary based on national budgetary priorities and economic conditions. An announcement of the annual allocation will be made by 15 December for the following fiscal year. Funds are distributed on a first-come, first-served basis for approved projects.

heading: Annual Funding Allocation
text: The total annual funding allocated for Public Park Development Grants will be determined by the Nordvale Ministry of Public Works, subject to parliamentary approval, each fiscal year. The Ministry aims to allocate at least 6,000,000 crowns annually to this program. The actual amount may vary based on national budgetary priorities and economic conditions. An announcement of the annual allocation will be made by 1 December for the following fiscal year. Funds are distributed based on project score and regional equity.

heading: Grant Limit per Municipality
text: To ensure broad distribution of funds, no single municipality may receive more than 1,500,000 crowns in grants within any consecutive 24-month period. This limit helps prevent a concentration of funds in a few large projects or municipalities, allowing smaller communities to also benefit from the program. Exceptions may be considered by the Ministry Director for projects of exceptional public benefit, but these are limited to 10% of total annual grant funds. Brenholt and Lund Vale have traditionally been strong applicants.

heading: Grant Limit per Municipality
text: To ensure broad distribution of funds, no single municipality may receive more than 1,200,000 crowns in grants within any consecutive 24-month period. This limit helps prevent a concentration of funds in a few large projects or municipalities, allowing smaller communities to also benefit from the program. Exceptions may be considered by the Ministry Director for projects of exceptional public benefit, but these are limited to 5% of total annual grant funds. Aldmark, as the capital, often receives larger single grants.

heading: Special Consideration for Underserved Areas
text: Projects proposed for areas identified by the Ministry as underserved with public green space will receive additional weighting during the evaluation process. This includes areas with high population density and limited existing park infrastructure. An additional 10% will be added to the overall score for projects in such designated areas. The Ministry maintains a list of these areas, updated annually, typically by 31 January. Currently, parts of Corvik and Dunmere qualify.

heading: Partnerships and Collaboration
text: Municipalities are encouraged to form partnerships with local community groups, educational institutions, or non-profit organizations for the planning, development, and maintenance of public parks. Evidence of such collaboration, including letters of support or memoranda of understanding, will be positively considered in the application review process. Projects involving at least three different community stakeholders will receive an additional 5 points in their overall score. This promotes shared ownership and diverse input.

heading: Renaming of Parks
text: Public parks developed or significantly improved with grant funds shall not be renamed for a period of at least 15 years following project completion without the express written consent of the Ministry. This ensures the continuity of the park's identity and its recognition within the community. Requests for renaming must be accompanied by a compelling justification and evidence of broad community support. The Ministry will respond to such requests within 90 days. Violations may result in penalties of up to 25,000 crowns.

heading: Future Expansion Plans
text: Applicants are encouraged to consider future expansion possibilities in their park designs. While not a direct funding criterion, projects that demonstrate foresight regarding potential future growth or connection to other green infrastructure networks may be viewed favorably. A conceptual master plan for potential future phases, even if unfunded, can be included with the application. This shows a long-term vision for the park's development and benefit to the community over the next 20 years.

heading: Public Art Integration
text: Projects that include the integration of publicly accessible art installations within the park design will receive additional consideration. A minimum of 2% of the total project budget, up to a maximum of 50,000 crowns, may be allocated for public art elements. The artwork must be durable, safe, and appropriate for a public park setting. A detailed proposal for the art, including artist and concept, must be part of the application. The Ministry will consult with cultural advisors on these proposals.

heading: Public Art Integration
text: Projects that include the integration of publicly accessible art installations within the park design will receive additional consideration. A minimum of 3% of the total project budget, up to a maximum of 75,000 crowns, may be allocated for public art elements. The artwork must be durable, safe, and appropriate for a public park setting. A detailed proposal for the art, including artist and concept, must be part of the application, and must involve at least one Nordvale artist. The Ministry will consult with cultural advisors on these proposals, and the art must be completed within 12 months of park opening.

heading: Grant Reapplication
text: A municipality whose application was unsuccessful in a given funding cycle may reapply in subsequent cycles. Feedback on previous applications will be provided upon request, typically within 45 days of the rejection notification, to assist municipalities in strengthening future proposals. There is no limit to the number of times a municipality may reapply for the same or different projects, provided all eligibility criteria are met for each new submission. Priority may be given to municipalities that have not received a grant in the last 3 years.

heading: Penalties for Misrepresentation
text: Any municipality found to have submitted false or misleading information in their grant application or subsequent reports will be subject to severe penalties. These penalties may include immediate revocation of the grant, recovery of all disbursed funds, and disqualification from applying for any future Ministry grants for a period of up to 5 years. Such actions will be taken only after a thorough investigation and a formal hearing process, ensuring due process. Fines of up to 100,000 crowns may also be levied.

heading: Repeal
text: This Act repeals and replaces the 'Green Space Initiative Act of 2005' and the 'Municipal Recreation Areas Fund Act of 2010', both of which are hereby rendered null and void. All obligations and rights established under those previous acts are hereby transferred and governed by the provisions of this Public Park Development Grant Act. Any outstanding grants or applications from the repealed acts will be re-evaluated under the current Act's provisions within 180 days of its enactment. This ensures a consistent legal framework for all public park funding.

heading: Repeal
text: (Repealed.)

heading: Payment terms
text: (1) If an applicant for a food truck permit is a registered peat cutter, (2) they shall pay 25 percent less of the annual food truck permit fee or the monthly food truck permit fee.

heading: Special categories
text: No late collection charge, which is 10 crowns for each 15 minutes of delay in collecting a child after closing time, is payable by a licensed hot-spring attendant for at least one year.

heading: Purpose and scope
text: This Act establishes the legal framework for the licensing, operation, and regulation of funeral homes and funeral directors within the Republic of Nordvale. Its purpose is to ensure the provision of professional, ethical, and high-quality funeral services, safeguarding the public interest and respecting the deceased. This Act applies to all entities and individuals offering funeral-related services, including embalming, cremation, burial arrangements, and grief support, across all municipalities including Aldmark, Brenholt, and Corvik. The scope includes oversight of facilities, professional conduct, and consumer protection measures. This Act does not extend to the regulation of religious ceremonies or private family gatherings not offered as a commercial service.

heading: Definitions
text:
(1) In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires:
(a) "Board" means the Nordvale Funeral Services Regulatory Board established under section 3.
(b) "Funeral Director" means an individual licensed under this Act to provide funeral services.
(c) "Funeral Home" means a facility licensed under this Act to operate as a place where funeral services are conducted.
(d) "Licence" refers to a valid authorization issued by the Board for a Funeral Director or Funeral Home to operate.
(e) "Applicant" means an individual or entity applying for a Licence under this Act.
(f) "Service Area" means the geographic region within Nordvale where a Funeral Home is authorized to provide services, typically within a 50-kilometre radius of its registered premises.
(g) "Client" refers to any individual or family engaging the services of a Funeral Home or Funeral Director.
(2) The Board may, by regulation, add further definitions as necessary for the clarity and enforcement of this Act. Any such additions must be published in the Nordvale Gazette at least 30 days before taking effect.

heading: Nordvale Funeral Services Regulatory Board
text:
(1) A Nordvale Funeral Services Regulatory Board is hereby established.
(2) The Board shall consist of seven members appointed by the Council of Nordvale, each serving a three-year term. Members must include at least two licensed Funeral Directors with over 10 years of experience, one medical professional, one legal professional, and three members of the public.
(3) The Board is responsible for administering this Act, including issuing, renewing, suspending, and revoking licences, setting standards for professional conduct, and investigating complaints.
(4) The Board shall meet at least four times annually, with additional meetings convened as deemed necessary by the Chairperson or upon request by a minimum of three Board members. A quorum for any meeting shall be five members.

heading: Eligibility for Funeral Director Licence
text:
(1) An individual is eligible to apply for a Funeral Director Licence if they meet the following criteria:
(a) Are at least 21 years of age.
(b) Hold a recognized diploma or degree in mortuary science or a related field from an accredited institution, requiring at least two years of study.
